title: Our World Landmarks

subtitle.text: Welcome, Little Fox readers. My name is Mr. Fay.
My students and I just started an exciting new social studies unit: world landmarks.
We're learning about some of the world's most famous places and buildings.
Each week Melissa, Jake, or Alex will tell you about what we discovered. We're glad that you can join us!
Yesterday was our first lesson. We studied the Grand Canyon, a huge canyon in the United States.
Melissa is going to tell you all about it.
So sit back and relax as you learn about this amazing place!
Hi everyone! As Mr. Fay said, yesterday our class learned about the Grand Canyon, located in the state of Arizona.
At first I thought it was going to be boring, but it wasn't at all!
Mr. Fay began with the story of how the canyon was made.
He said that millions of years ago, a river began flowing over layers of stone.
This river—known today as the Colorado River—made grooves in the sheets of rock that grew deeper and wider.
Over time the rock became a long valley with steep walls: the Grand Canyon.
Some rocks in the canyon are about 2.5 billion years old.
Because the canyon is so old, there are some really interesting things in the rocks, like ancient shells.
You can also find other cool fossils, like ones of sponges, fish teeth, and animal footprints.
In the twentieth century, scientists found something else in the canyon: small twig figures shaped like deer and other animals.
Scientists think these figures are thousands of years old.
The figures show that humans, especially Native Americans, have been living in the Grand Canyon region for a very long time.
Europeans and Americans didn't really know much about the canyon until 1869.
That's when an American geologist named John Wesley Powell decided to lead the first official river expedition through the canyon.
Powell and his men faced many hardships, especially treacherous currents and harsh weather.
It must have been extra hard for Powell because, guess what? He only had one arm!
As the men explored, they took pictures, studied rocks, and drew maps. Then they shared the canyon with the world.
Powell even named it, calling it the Grand Canyon because of its size and magnificent beauty.
In 1919 the U.S. government turned the Grand Canyon into a national park to protect the canyon's wildlife and landscape.
Now almost five million people go to Arizona each year to visit Grand Canyon National Park.
Mr. Fay said the best way to see the canyon is by hiking.
The park has short walks along the canyon's edge, but it also has a 34-kilometer hike that goes along the bottom of the entire canyon. 34 kilometers!
If you're like me and just the thought of walking that far wears you out, you can see the canyon in other ways—such as by helicopter, boat, or mule. (Personally I'd choose the helicopter!)
If you do go hiking down to the bottom, be sure to take plenty of water, sunscreen, and a map.
Also be prepared for all kinds of weather.
Mr. Fay said the canyon is so deep that the weather changes drastically as you descend.
When he visited in the winter, he was hiking along through some snow near the rim.
But later, when he reached the bottom, it was hot and sunny!
Next Mr. Fay showed us pictures of animals that live in the canyon today.
We saw photos of bighorn sheep standing on rocky cliffs, beavers chomping on trees, and eagles soaring in the sky.
Mr. Fay also showed us pictures of scary animals, like coyotes and mountain lions.
He said to watch out for coyotes especially because they'll come right into your campsite looking for food.
Some other scary animals in the canyon are rattlesnakes and scorpions.
I didn't like seeing pictures of them. They give me the creeps!
One animal we learned a lot about was the California condor, the largest flying bird in North America.
I was really sad when I found out that condors are endangered.
In 1987 there were less than ten left in the whole world!
But thanks to the work of conservationists, California condors are returning to the Grand Canyon, and their numbers are rising.
Mr. Fay actually got to see one when he visited.
He said that when condors fly, their gigantic, flapping wings make the sound of thunder!
The Grand Canyon is really amazing. However, like a lot of Earth's beautiful natural landmarks, it is also in danger.
Because of pollution and tourism, the land is being worn down and animal habitats are being destroyed.
Luckily some groups are working to protect the canyon—and you can help too.
If you're ever there, be sure to pick up your trash, stay on the marked paths, leave the wild animals alone, and tell others to do the same.
After we finished learning about the Grand Canyon, our class made a big mural of it.
My friends painted a condor flying over the canyon and a one-armed man in a boat on the river. I added myself, waving from a helicopter.
I think our teacher described the Grand Canyon best.
He said it's like "a book that tells the history of the earth."
I know what he meant now: the layers of the canyon's ancient walls hold the story of life on our planet. What an awesome place!
That's all for now, everyone. I wonder what our next landmarks lesson will be about. I guess we'll find out together next week!
Hey, Little Fox readers! I'm Jake. Yesterday in Mr. Fay's class we learned about the Louvre, one of the biggest art museums in the whole world.
I love to draw, so I was pretty excited when I heard we'd be learning about an art museum in France.
And I'm not the only one who gets excited about art.
Mr. Fay told us that 8.5 million people from all over the world visit the Louvre each year.
Now that's what I call a lot of visitors!
The Louvre is located in the heart of Paris, on the right bank of the Seine River.
It's home to around 35,000 pieces of art and nearly 13 kilometers of galleries.
That means it would take almost a year for a visitor to see everything inside the museum!
When the Louvre was first built, way back in 1190, it was designed to be a fortress to protect Paris from its enemies. At
the time Paris was the largest city in Europe, and over the next two hundred years, the city continued to grow. Eventually
the Louvre wasn't big enough to protect the entire city. So,
in 1364, King Charles V decided to turn it into a palace. During

the centuries that followed, members of the French royalty continued changing the Louvre, demolishing some sections and adding new buildings and wings, along with gardens and fancy decorations. French
monarchs also collected artwork, filling the Louvre with colorful tapestries, elaborate carvings, and all kinds of incredible paintings. Eventually
the royal court decided to move to a new palace, abandoning the Louvre for a while. Finally,
in 1793, government officials decided to turn the buildings into a museum for the public. Today
the Louvre has three main wings. They're
arranged like a giant horseshoe, and in the courtyard in the middle of the wings is a big glass pyramid. Inside
the Louvre, visitors can see art from many different time periods. There's
a helmet worn by a real Roman gladiator; Egyptian statues over 4000 years old; and a sword used at the coronations of French kings. Mr.
Fay also showed us some pictures of mummies at the museum. Melissa
said they looked really creepy, but I thought they looked really cool! Most
people visiting the Louvre stop to see the most famous painting in the world—the Mona Lisa .
It's a small portrait of a woman, painted by Leonardo da Vinci in 1506.
One reason the painting is famous is because da Vinci's brushwork makes the background look very realistic.
But the main reason for the Mona Lisa 's popularity is probably the mysterious smile on the woman's
face. A lot of people think she's smiling because she has a secret. Hmm . . . What do you think?
On August 21, 1911, a former worker at the Louvre, Vincenzo Peruggia, actually managed to steal the Mona Lisa
. Peruggia went to the museum one day, pretending to be a
visitor. When the museum closed for the night, he hid and slept there
overnight. The next morning he simply removed the painting from the wall, concealed it under his clothing, and walked out the
door! I guess they didn't have any high-tech security cameras or alarms back
then. The Mona Lisa wasn't found until two years later, when Peruggia made the mistake of trying to sell it to an antiques dealer who reported him to the
police. Ever since then the Mona Lisa has been kept behind some very strong
glass. But it still attracts huge crowds, with thousands of visitors trying to catch a glimpse of the mysterious woman every
day. The Raft of the Medusa by Théodore Géricault is another well-known painting at the
Louvre. But this isn't one you could sneak out of a museum—it's almost five meters high and over seven meters
wide! I found out that in 1939, the painting's enormous size caused an enormous
problem. World War II had begun, and museum workers were worried about the valuable artwork inside the
Louvre. So they decided to pack it up and move it to castles around France for
safekeeping. Workers placed The Raft of the Medusa on the back of an open
truck. On the drive out to the countryside, the tall painting knocked down some electrical
wires. This caused the electricity to go out in an entire
city! Another popular item at the Louvre is the Venus de Milo, a marble statue that was discovered by
accident. In 1820 a farmer on the island of Melos was digging in the ground when he uncovered a statue in two pieces.
The whole statue was carefully dug out, and then presented to King Louis XVIII of France.
The king later donated it to the Louvre.
Experts believe that the Venus de Milo was carved sometime around 100 BC.
The statue is most likely of Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and beauty.
But nobody knows this for sure because the statue is missing some parts, including its arms.
Last night I went to the library and brought home a book about the Louvre.
It has pictures of some of the artwork at the museum, and I practiced drawing a bunch of things.
Oh, and I also created my own drawing.
Check it out: it's a picture of Vincenzo Peruggia stealing the Mona Lisa while being chased by an Egyptian mummy!
I hope you enjoyed learning more about the Louvre.
See you again soon for another landmarks lesson!
Hi, everyone. My name is Alex. Mr. Fay just told us about the tallest mountain on Earth—Mount Everest.
I can't wait to tell you about it because this lesson changed my life! But more about that later.
Mount Everest is part of the Himalayas, a huge mountain range in Asia.
The Himalayas are known as the roof of the world because many of the world's biggest mountains are here.
Mount Everest, the tallest of them all, is about 8,848 meters high.
Its summit is the highest point on Earth!
Mount Everest is shaped like a three-sided pyramid.
Two of these sides face Tibet, near China. The other side faces Nepal, near India.
People in the Western world didn't really know much about Mount Everest until the 1920s.
That's when British troops were sent to explore the Himalayas and discover a route to Everest's summit.
But this expedition failed; and so did the next; and the next after that.
Finally in 1953 Sir Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay, a Nepalese guide, became the first people to stand on Mount Everest's peak.
Since then over ten thousand people have tried to reach the summit.
Thousands have succeeded, but hundreds of others have died while trying.
Each of Mount Everest's three sides can be climbed, but the south side facing Nepal is the most popular.
Mr. Fay said it usually takes 64 days to climb this side!
An expedition on Mount Everest is hard work.
Climbers have to travel over slippery rocks and sheets of ice as well as steep inclines and bottomless crevasses. Death is always possible.
It takes a long time to prepare for a climb. For the first few days, climbers get ready in Kathmandu, the capital of Nepal.
They meet the other members of their team, make sure they have everything they need, and hire porters to help carry the equipment.
Most of the porters are Sherpa, Nepalese people who live in the valleys of the Himalayas.
Without the help of the Sherpa and their yaks, most climbers wouldn't make it to the summit.
When Sir Hillary climbed Mount Everest back in 1953, he said he felt like an ant in a giant's world.
I can just imagine being surrounded by towering mounds of snow, ancient glaciers, and the majestic mountains of the Himalayas.
That would make me feel pretty small too!
Many people used to think that gods and demons lived in the mountains—along with a huge, ape-like monster called the Abominable Snowman.
There are lots of stories about how giant footprints in the snow were made by the Abominable Snowman.
Others say the footprints were made by bears. But who knows?
The leading cause of death on Mount Everest is not the Abominable Snowman, but avalanches.
Huge sections of the mountain can suddenly break off and slide down at speeds of over three hundred kilometers per hour, crushing and burying everything in their path!
Also the glaciers that cover parts of the mountain sometimes move, causing deep cracks to form in the ice.
There are other dangers too, including low levels of oxygen that make climbers tired and dizzy.
Frostbite occurs when fingers, toes, or facial parts freeze.
In really serious cases, the frostbitten body parts have to be cut off—yikes!
Some people are reminded of these dangers when they stumble across frozen dead bodies, the remains of other climbers who perished on Mount Everest.
Reaching the summit takes a lot of courage and hard work.
But for serious mountain climbers, there's no bigger dream than standing on top of Everest.
Over the years climbers have done some incredible things.
For example, in 1980 Reinhold Messner became the first man to climb to the peak completely alone.
Several people have skied or snowboarded down from the summit.
In 2001 a man named Erik Weihenmayer became the first blind man to stand on the top. Pretty awesome, huh?
And in 2010 Jordan Romero became the youngest person to reach the summit—at thirteen years old! That's around my age!
Now for the bad news. Unfortunately Mount Everest's popularity with climbers has taken its toll both on the slopes and in the valleys below.
On the slopes, litter is a serious problem. It interferes with climbers' expeditions and it pollutes a really cool world landmark.
There have been some major clean-up operations, and workers have brought back thousands of pounds of trash, including oxygen containers, tents, food wrappers, and human waste.
The Nepalese side of Mount Everest and the valleys below it are part of Sagarmatha National Park.
Because of deforestation, many animals in the valleys, such as snow leopards and Tibetan bears, have lost their homes.
Massive numbers of trees are being cut down to provide enough firewood and construction material for all the climbers who pass through the region.
Many people are aware of the deforestation issue.
Local and international organizations are working hard to preserve and restore Mount Everest and its surrounding areas.
For example, climbers are now encouraged to use kerosene instead of wood for fuel.
And each year over a million seedlings are planted in the valleys to replace those that were cut down.
Organizations and workers are optimistic that the area will soon recover.
Now I'll tell you why this lesson changed my life.
I've found my life goal—to stand on top of the world someday, on the summit of Mount Everest!
I guess I should start practicing my mountain climbing.
Too bad there aren't many mountains around here!
Hi, Little Fox readers! I have to go downstairs soon and help my little brother with his science project.
But first I want to tell you about another really cool landmark: Pompeii.
It's an ancient city on the west coast of Italy that is one of the oldest and largest archaeological sites in the world.
Unfortunately it's also famous because of a terrible tragedy.
In 79 AD it was totally wiped out by a volcano!
Pompeii was built right at the foot of Mount Vesuvius sometime during the sixth century BC.
I asked Mr. Fay why the people of Pompeii built their city so close to an active volcano.
Mr. Fay said they had never seen Mount Vesuvius erupt so they just assumed it would be safe.
But it wasn't.
Mount Vesuvius had been quiet for almost a thousand years. But when a volcano goes without erupting for a long time like that, pressure builds up inside it.
On the morning of August 24, this built-up pressure finally caused a massive eruption.
Mr. Fay told us about a Roman writer named Pliny the Younger who recorded what happened that day.
According to Pliny, a towering cloud of smoke and volcanic debris filled the sky.
Hot rocks rained down on the city all day long as people hid inside buildings.
The next morning there was a huge explosion.
That's when a deadly wave of cinders and burning-hot gas swept over Pompeii.
The whole city, including thousands of people, was buried under six meters of volcanic ash!
I bet you're wondering the same thing I was wondering: Why is an ancient city that was completely destroyed by a volcano still a famous landmark?
Well, in 1748, after Pompeii had been buried for 17 centuries, the king of Spain began organizing digs there, hoping to find valuable artwork.
Soon others began digging too—and taking whatever they found.
Finally, in 1860, an archaeologist named Giuseppe Fiorelli put a stop to all the careless digging by developing a new system for keeping track of what was uncovered.
Fiorelli also made sure that the buildings were handled more carefully.
For the first time, workers dug out the buildings by starting at the top and working their way down.
This was a much better way of preserving what was found.
Some workers at the site discovered open cavities in the hardened ash and mud.
They realized that these were spaces left behind after buried bodies decayed.
So Fiorelli came up with a clever idea—to pour plaster into these spaces.
Once the plaster dried, workers could chip away the hardened ash and mud, revealing casts of the buried people.
If you ask me, these casts are amazing, but pretty creepy too.
You can tell from looking at the casts that the people were crouching down or clinging to family members when they were buried alive.
And you can see in the people's faces just how scared they were.
Because of Fiorelli's work, scholars have learned a lot about daily life in ancient Pompeii.
It was once a bustling, prosperous city with temples, theaters, bathhouses, restaurants, and factories for making wool and tools.
And get this: workers at the site also found bakeries—with bread still sitting in the ovens!
Inscriptions on buildings, tablets, tombs, and the bases of statues gave scholars even more information about life in Pompeii.
A banker's tablets revealed how people made business transactions.
Writings on walls supplied details about things like politics, gladiator battles—even falling in love!
Today Pompeii is open to the public all year long.
Mr. Fay said that it's one of Italy's most popular tourist attractions, and that going there is like stepping back in time.
You can see some of the plaster casts that were made from buried victims.
You can also stroll along the narrow streets and alleyways, just as people did two thousand years ago, and look at the ancient stone walls and columns.
I read that you can go inside many of the buildings too, and imagine what it was like to live in one of the houses, eat at a restaurant, or perform in a theater!
I learned that Pompeii is so well-preserved because it was buried for such a long time under hardened ash and mud.
But unfortunately, after being constantly exposed to crowds of tourists and harsh weather, Pompeii has suffered a lot of damage.
An entire building, the House of the Gladiators, completely collapsed in 2010.
Now all that's left of this ancient site, where mighty gladiators once prepared for battle, is a huge pile of rubble. I think that's really sad.
I wanted to know if people living near Pompeii today have to worry about Mount Vesuvius erupting again. After all, it's still a volcano!
Mr. Fay said that Mount Vesuvius has erupted many times since August 24, 79 AD, but never as violently as on that day.
And today scientists know a lot more about volcanoes.
Before a volcano erupts, there are usually warning signs—like a water supply drying up or an earthquake—so scientists can monitor volcanoes for any dangerous activity.
Whew! I felt a lot better after Mr. Fay told us this.
If Mount Vesuvius were about to erupt again, people could be warned months ahead of time.
Well, I hope you enjoyed learning about Pompeii. I know I did!
I've got to go help my brother now.
He's making something really cool for a science project. Guess what it is? That's right; a volcano!
Hey, Little Fox readers. It's me again, Jake. And I've got some questions for you.
What is the world's smallest continent and sixth-largest country?
Where can you find wild kangaroos, koalas, and wombats? That's right—Australia!
Last year my parents went to Australia for their wedding anniversary.
When they came back, they showed me pictures of a cool building in Sydney, the largest city in Australia.
Guess what—the building turned out to be the landmark we studied in Mr. Fay's class yesterday!
The Sydney Opera House is one of the most photographed buildings in the world.
I found out that it's on the UNESCO World Heritage List, which means it's a very important world landmark.
Most of the other landmarks on the list, like the pyramids of Egypt and the Great Wall of China, are really ancient.
But the Sydney Opera House, completed in 1973, is the youngest site to be included on the list.
The reason the Sydney Opera House became such a famous landmark is because of its very unusual design.
The roofs were designed to look like billowing sails—perfect for its location in Sydney Harbor.
Mr. Fay said that many people consider the building a modern-day masterpiece!
In 1956 the government in Sydney held a competition for the best design of a new performance center.
Over two hundred entries—including one from a Danish architect named Jorn Utzon—came in from all over the world.
According to one story, Utzon's design was almost thrown out.
Luckily it was rescued by a judge who arrived late.
As the judge was looking through entries discarded by other judges, he found Utzon's design and wondered why it had been rejected.
He thought it was amazing! This judge convinced the others to take another look, and on January 29, 1957, Utzon was announced the winner.
Once construction began, Utzon and his team of builders realized that it would be very difficult to turn the design into a real building.
The shells Utzon wanted to use for the roof turned out to be particularly challenging.
Utzon wanted the shells to be white, like sails or clouds.
But he also didn't want to blind people when the sun reflected off the roof.
Utzon eventually found the perfect inspiration: Japanese ceramic bowls.
The clay used to make these bowls was light-colored but rough enough to keep the bowls from being too shiny.
He asked a Swedish ceramic company to invent a special tile that was similar to the Japanese bowls.
This new tile, called Sydney tile, was made from clay and crushed stone.
It took over a million tiles and several years to create the shells.
Then in 1965, just after the shells had finally been finished, a new government official was put in charge of the project.
This official didn't really like the building's design, and he thought the project was too expensive.
Eventually he persuaded the government to stop paying Utzon. So in 1966 Utzon quit.
Many people thought the official's actions were unfair.
They held protests and marches on the streets of Sydney, asking the government to give Utzon back his job.
But the government refused. Utzon and his family returned to Europe, and a new architectural team was chosen to complete the building.
By the time the Sydney Opera House opened in October of 1973, many changes had been made to the original design.
I'm an artist myself, so I bet Utzon was pretty sad about what happened!
Jorn Utzon wasn't forgotten though. In 1999, after a series of conversations and meetings, Utzon returned as the opera house's architect.
His first major project was to redo the reception hall, now called the Utzon Room in his honor.
It's the only hall in the whole opera house that is completely true to Utzon's own design.
In 2003 Utzon received the highest honor in international architecture, the Pritzker Prize, for his many accomplishments, including his imaginative design of the Sydney Opera House.
The Sydney Opera House is really big. It has seven main performance halls, which include an opera theater, a concert hall, a playhouse, and an outdoor concert area.
As you can tell from these different halls, the Sydney Opera House isn't just for opera lovers.
Each year there are over 1,500 programs, which feature individuals and groups from all over the world.
Performances include ethnic dance groups, symphony orchestras, rock-and-roll concerts, plays, and ballets. There are even movies and puppet shows!
Mr. Fay also told us about Le Grande Cirque, an amazing circus that performs at the Sydney Opera House.
Usually I think circuses are for little kids, but this one sounds really awesome.
For one of the acts, performers zoom around on motorcycles inside a huge, ball-shaped cage!
Over a million people attend these events each year.
But over seven million come to the Sydney Opera House just to see the site.
There are tours offered every day in at least seven different languages.
There is also a two-hour long backstage tour.
My parents said that sometimes visitors are allowed to do cool things, like stand on the stage in the concert hall or visit the stars' dressing rooms.
When I got home from school, I asked my parents if I could see their photograph of the Sydney Opera House again.
As soon as I saw it, I had an idea. I rushed up to my room and drew a picture of the opera house.
But I added one thing: a statue of Jorn Utzon, sketching by the harbor.
I think it looks great there. Who knows? Someday my design could become a real statue!
Hi, again, Little Fox readers. It's Alex. I'm back to tell you about an awesome landmark that we just learned about in Mr. Fay's class: the Amazon River.
Have you ever heard of it? If not, get ready to be impressed!
Here are some of the coolest things about it: First, the Amazon is the longest river in South America and the biggest river in the world because it holds the most water.
Second, the Earth's most unique rain forest lies in the Amazon's basin, which is the land around a river.
And the third coolest thing about it is . . . Wait, I'm going to save that one for last!
The Amazon River runs from the Andes Mountains in Peru to the coast of the Atlantic Ocean in Brazil.
Mr. Fay says river channels change all the time, so it's hard to figure out the Amazon's exact length.
But it's usually considered to be about 6,400 kilometers long.
It carries about one-fifth of all the river water on Earth.
That's more water than the Nile, Mississippi, Yangtze, and Ganges Rivers combined!
How did it get to be so huge?
Well, the Amazon drains an area that is nearly as big as the United States, and in its southern parts, the rainy season can last nearly half the year.
In class Mr. Fay showed us a book about how the Amazon got its name. It's a pretty interesting story.
Although South American natives have lived on the shores of the Amazon for around 12,000 years, Europeans didn't discover it until about 500 years ago.
In 1541 a Spanish explorer named Francisco de Orellana was sent to look for land to conquer, and he ended up on the Amazon.
His 3,017-kilometer journey on the river made him the first European to navigate its dangerous waters.
But it was no easy expedition.
Apparently Orellana and his men were attacked by native female warriors who lived along the river.
These women were fierce, fighting off Orellana's party with bows and arrows.
According to Orellana each woman had the strength of ten men!
He was so impressed by them that he called them the Amazons after the female warriors in Greek mythology.
Later the same name was given to the mighty river where Orellana had encountered these women.
It wasn't until much later, though, that people discovered all the natural resources along the Amazon River basin—like fish, Brazil nuts, and animal skins—and flocked to it.
In the mid-1800s a rubber boom brought the first huge wave of North Americans and Europeans to the area.
Did you know that rubber comes from trees?
People put taps in the tree trunks to extract latex, the same way people collect maple syrup from maple trees.
Then the latex is turned into rubber. And the good thing is that extracting latex doesn't hurt the tree at all.
Anyway, the rubber tree is one of the most common trees in the Amazon rain forest, and the North Americans and Europeans were very excited when they discovered it.
They saw that they could make waterproof tires, shoes, and other things with this new material.
Unfortunately, in their quest for rubber, they killed many of the natives and cut down lots of trees to power their steamboats.
This was the beginning of the destruction of the Amazon.
Today huge sections of the Amazon rain forest are being cleared for logging and cattle ranching.
This harms both the rain forest and the river.
When there are no trees to shade the ground, the land and river channels dry up more quickly.
Areas that were once rich with plant and animal life are now barren deserts. I couldn't believe it when I read that!
Luckily, a lot of organizations are working hard to preserve what's left.
Scientists think that more than a third of the world's plant and animal species live in the Amazon River basin.
Can you imagine how horrible it would be if they disappeared?
We learned about lots of different plants and animals that live in the rain forest, but I think the really big animals are the most interesting.
There's the anaconda, the world's largest snake, which can grow to be over ten meters long.
But it isn't the only giant predator lurking in the river.
There's also the black caiman, a six-meter long crocodile.
The black caiman is endangered because it was once intensely hunted for its skin.
Now its numbers are slowly on the rise because anti-hunting laws were put in place.
In the meantime I bet the animals it preys on are happy!
These include the capybara, a huge rodent, and the piranha, a vicious fish.
By now you probably want to know how you can visit the Amazon River and the amazing rain forest around it.
According to experts the best way is definitely by boat.
Lots of cargo ships still ride down the river, and you can catch a ride on one of those and sleep in a hammock on the deck.
But I'm sure tour boats would be more comfortable.
If I went, I would go on a week-long tour that starts in Iquitos, Peru.
Iquitos is near the Andes Mountains, and it's the largest city in South America that can't be reached by roads.
That sounds pretty awesome to me.
But if you don't like boats, you can stay at one of the hotels along the riverbank.
Now are you ready to learn the third coolest thing about the Amazon?
It's the Great River Amazon Raft Race, the longest raft race in the world!
Teams from all over the globe paddle down the river on homemade, wooden rafts.
The race is 180 kilometers long and lasts for three days!
I hope I get to compete in the raft race one day.
I can already picture myself swatting mosquitoes and wiping sweat off my face as I paddle down the Amazon!
Welcome back, Little Fox Readers. I was really excited about this week's landmark because it's in London, England—the city I'll be visiting this summer with my family!
Mr. Fay taught us all about the Tower of London, one of the most famous castles in the world.
The Tower of London started out as just one tall, square-shaped fortress known as the White Tower, which was built almost a thousand years ago.
Over time British kings expanded this fortress by constructing more towers and walls around the White Tower.
Today this entire complex of buildings and walls is known as the Tower of London, or just the Tower.
Medieval kings used the Tower as a royal residence.
They also stored weapons and valuables there, along with exotic animals like lions and bears.
Sometimes these animals were allowed to wander around outside.
King Henry III's polar bear, for example, was put on a long chain so it could go fishing in the Thames River.
I bet the locals were pretty terrified!
Around 1100 the Tower began being used as a prison.
The first prisoner to be kept there was Bishop Ranulf Flambard, a tax collector who found a clever way to escape.
Flambard had some friends deliver a gallon of wine with a rope hidden inside.
On the day of a special feast, he invited his guards to celebrate and have some wine.
Then when the guards fell asleep, he used the rope to climb out the window!
For many centuries after that, the Tower continued serving as a prison.
Mr. Fay told us stories about some of the most famous and interesting prisoners, like Queen Anne Boleyn, who was beheaded for failing to give birth to a son;
Hew Draper, who was accused of practicing sorcery and left an intricate astrological carving on his cell wall;
and Guy Fawkes, an explosives expert who tried to blow up the entire ruling class, including the royal family!
One story was very sad—and scary. Prince Edward V and his younger brother, Richard, were sent to the Tower in 1483.
They were only twelve and ten years old.
Their uncle, the Duke of Gloucester, had imprisoned the princes so that they wouldn't interfere with his becoming king.
And here's the really spooky part: the boys were never seen again.
Most people think they were murdered because many years later, two child-sized skeletons were discovered near the White Tower.
By the 1800s the Tower wasn't being used much as a prison or royal residence anymore.
An architect named Anthony Salvin was hired to restore it to its medieval appearance and make it more suitable for tourists.

Salvin renovated buildings and rooms, making it easier to see graffiti written by prisoners on cell walls and creating a place to showcase the crown jewels, a collection of precious ornaments worn by British royalty.
After these renovations the number of tourists at the Tower grew quickly.
By 1901 over half a million people were visiting each year, and today that number is close to two million.
When my family and I go to London, we're definitely going to spend at least a day there.
My dad and little brother want to see the royal armor that's on display in the White Tower.
According to my dad, some of the armor was worn by kings five hundred years ago!
The royal armor sounds cool, but my first stop is definitely going to be the Jewel House, where the crown jewels are kept.
Mr. Fay said that there are more than 23,000 gems in the collection, mostly found on scepters and crowns.
One of the most famous items is the Imperial State Crown, which is decorated with over three thousand gems, including diamonds, pearls, rubies, and sapphires.
The royals still wear some of these crowns, but I won't be able to try anything on: security is very tight!
I also want to see the yeoman warders—soldiers who are part of the Royal Bodyguard.
According to legend these soldiers were once allowed to eat as much beef as they wanted from the king's table.
And so they became known as beefeaters.
Many visitors go on tours given by the yeoman warders.
The yeoman warders relate the history of the Tower, including gory stories of torture and executions of prisoners.
They even tell stories about ghosts that supposedly haunt the Tower to this day!
The yeoman warders and their families actually get to live in the Tower. Pretty awesome, huh?
And they share their home with some very important creatures: the Tower ravens.
In the seventeenth century, King Charles II decreed that there must always be at least six ravens living at the Tower.
Legend says that if the ravens ever leave the Tower, both the Tower and the kingdom of England will fall!
In recent years there have been six ravens living at the Tower, along with at least one or two extra birds.
The Ravenmaster, a special yeoman warder, cares for these birds, who are very intelligent and can live for many years.
Their wings are clipped so that they can't fly too far away, and visitors often spot them on the grounds.
I hope I get to see a few when I visit the Tower!
Last night I had to babysit my brother, and we pretended we were living in the Tower.
I made a crown and scepter for myself and pretended to be the queen of England.
My brother made a sword and some armor and pretended to be a knight.
He rescued me from an evil dragon—the vacuum cleaner—and bravely battled it until Mom and Dad got home.
I really liked learning about the Tower of London in Mr. Fay's class.
Now I really can't wait until summertime. London, here I come!
Hey there, Little Fox readers! It's me, Jake, again.
Last week I watched a cool movie that takes place at a temple deep in the jungle.
The next day Mr. Fay said we'd be learning about a new landmark called Angkor Wat.
And when he showed us a picture of it, I recognized it right away. It was the temple from the movie!
Angkor Wat is an ancient Buddhist temple located in Angkor, Cambodia.
It's famous for its carved sandstone towers and for being one of the largest religious structures in the whole world.
Angkor Wat is also considered a really important work of architecture from the Khmer Empire.
Mr. Fay said that this powerful empire covered most of Southeast Asia and it flourished from the ninth to thirteenth centuries.
That was when Khmer rulers built many cities and villages, along with canals, roads, palaces, and temples.
In the twelfth century, a king named Suryavarman II ordered the construction of Angkor Wat.
It was built to serve as both a temple for the Hindu god Vishnu and a massive tomb for the king himself.
Over time Buddhism spread, and by the thirteenth century, it was the official religion of the Khmers.
Many of the Khmer temples, including Angkor Wat, were converted to Buddhist temples.
Nobody is quite sure why, but sometime in the fifteenth century, the Khmers abandoned Angkor and moved their capital to Phnom Penh.
Except for a small number of Buddhist monks who stayed behind, Angkor was forgotten until a French explorer, Henri Mouhot, traveled to the site.
Mouhot wrote about Angkor and created some ink drawings of the temples that got other people interested in them too.
Today hundreds of the Khmer temples can still be seen in the area known as Angkor Archaeological Park.
Angkor Wat is definitely the most famous temple there.
And as Mr. Fay told us, it's also the biggest temple, covering about 2.6 square kilometers.
In fact, its name, Angkor Wat, means "city temple." So it is one huge place!
Angkor Wat is Cambodia's busiest tourist attraction, with close to a million visitors each year.
It's also an important visiting place for Buddhist monks.
If you're ever lucky enough to go, try to get there early.
I heard that it's pretty awesome to see the sun rise from behind the temple's tall towers!
To enter the temple, visitors first have to cross an enormous moat that surrounds the entire complex.
Today this moat is filled with lily pads and lotus blossoms, but Mr. Fay said it probably once had crocodiles too.
I bet nobody ever went swimming in there!
The temple itself has nine towers; each one is shaped like a giant lotus blossom.
Four outer towers surround the five main inner ones.
The center inner tower is the tallest of all and sits on top of the temple's main shrine. For
most people, climbing the steep steps to the top of the temple is quite a workout. And
it can be dangerous and slippery too. The temple's builders had a good reason for making this such a treacherous climb. The
five inner towers symbolize the five peaks of Mount Meru, the home of the Hindu gods. Walking
up those steps is supposed to be like ascending to where the gods and goddesses live! At
the top of the steps, visitors can tour the temple's corridors and shrines. Many
people enjoy seeing the famous bas-reliefs, or shallow carvings, in the temple walls. Some
depict historic battles, like the Battle of Kurukshetra, which had soldiers fighting alongside elephants and horse-drawn chariots. Other
bas-reliefs show scenes of everyday life or King Suryavarman II's court. The
most famous bas-relief in Angkor Wat has a scene from Hindu mythology. It's
called Churning of the Sea of Milk , and it shows gods and demons in what looks like an epic game of tug-of-war.
But really they are trying to create a special potion for eternal life.
And it isn't a rope they are tugging on—it's a giant snake! Pretty awesome, huh?
Angkor Wat is still an amazing place, but it has faced some threats over the years.
During the centuries that Angkor was abandoned, the surrounding jungle grew all around the temples, hiding them from sight.
Today the roots of huge banyan trees are still wrapped around some of the structures at Angkor Archaeological Park.
I like the way the giant roots look, but Mr. Fay said they can do serious damage over time, cracking the stone and even causing sections of the temples to topple over.
The outer walls of Angkor Wat have also been damaged by bullet holes from all the fighting that took place during Cambodia's civil war in the late twentieth century.
The fighting made the area around Angkor very dangerous, giving thieves the chance to steal valuables from the temples.
Believe it or not, entire statues were carried away, and large sections of bas-reliefs were chiseled right off the walls!
I was glad to hear that many people are working hard today to protect and restore Angkor Wat, along with the other temples at Angkor Archaeological Park.
Security officers patrol the site to keep out thieves while scholars from around the world carefully repair and maintain the ancient ruins.
And the people of Cambodia are still very proud of their beautiful temple.
Angkor Wat appears on some of the country's money—and on its national flag!
When I watched that movie the other day, I thought it was pretty cool to see spies tracking each other down inside an ancient temple.
But you know what's even cooler? The real Angkor Wat!
Hi, Little Fox readers! We've been learning about the environment, so Mr. Fay told us about a landmark that goes perfectly with this topic—Easter Island.
Also known as Rapa Nui, this island in the South Pacific is the most remote inhabited island in the world.
And it's famous for something else: hundreds of huge, mysterious statues called moai
. At first I couldn't imagine how a tiny island with a bunch of statues is connected to taking care of the
environment. But I found out that these statues have a lot to do with the
environment. I'll get to that in a minute. First let me tell you about the island itself—it has a really interesting
history! Easter Island was first settled by Polynesians sometime around 400 AD.
The island's landscape is very sparse now, but when those settlers, now called the Rapanui, first arrived in their canoes, the whole island was covered in palm trees.
Nobody is sure why these people came to the island. I'm amazed that they even found it because it's small—only 163 square kilometers.
And it's in the middle of nowhere, almost 2,000 kilometers from Pitcairn Island, the nearest land.
Over time the Rapanui changed the island's landscape by cutting down trees and clearing the land to plant crops.
And between 1000 and 1680 AD, they transformed the landscape in another dramatic way—by sculpting hundreds of moai and placing them all over the island.
The Rapanui carved the moai out of yellowish-gray volcanic rock.
The heads look a little creepy but cool too, with long noses and ears, and protruding foreheads above deep-set eyes.
Archaeologists believe these statues depict important Rapanui ancestors and chiefs.
Some of the moai also have round topknots on top of their heads.
The topknots look like big red hats because they're made from red volcanic rock.
Most of the moai were carved out of the bedrock of the volcano Rano Raraku.
First, sculptors shaped the statues' faces and heads. When that was done, the statues were cut free from the surrounding rock.
Next, they were lowered down the slope of the volcano and propped up vertically in shallow holes so the backs could be carved. Today
there are 397 moai remaining at Rano Raraku. Some
are still attached to the bedrock, including one that's over 20 meters long! Others
are standing up in those shallow holes. But because of silt running down the slope of the volcano over so many years, they're partially buried. Completed
moai had to be moved to various villages around the island. This
must have been extremely difficult since the average moai was over 4 meters tall and weighed over 12 metric tons. Moving
one probably required between 50 and 150 people! Nobody
knows for sure exactly how the moai were moved. Many
people believe they were placed on wooden sleds that were towed with ropes, while others believe that the statues were tilted slightly and then "walked" across the island. My
favorite theory is one that Mr. Fay told us, from an island legend: The moai got up and walked by themselves! Once
moved, moai were placed on rectangular stone platforms. Most
of these platforms were placed near the coast, overlooking villages. Each
one had between one and fifteen moai standing in a row, with their backs to the sea. These
moai were given eyes made from shells and polished stones. The
Rapanui had no contact with other people until Easter Sunday, 1722, when a Dutch explorer named Jacob Roggeveen arrived on the island and started calling it Easter Island. Roggeveen wrote
that the islanders worshipped the moai . He
also wrote that, unlike most Polynesian islands, Easter Island had almost no trees, just small shrubs and grass. Sometime
after Roggeveen's arrival, a civil war broke out on the island, probably because of overpopulation and limited resources. The
Rapanui stopped making moai and even started knocking each others' down! Today
Easter Island is part of Rapa Nui National Park. Visitors can get there from Santiago, Chile. Almost
everyone on the island lives in Hanga Roa, the island's only town, which has some hotels, restaurants, and shops. Mr.
Fay said that there are about nine hundred moai still scattered all over the island, so it's a good idea to hire a guide who can show you around. One
very popular site for tourists is the quarry at Rano Raraku, where you can see the unfinished moai .
I bet you're still wondering what Easter Island has to do with the environment.
Well, many experts believe the Rapanui continued cutting down trees to use as firewood and building materials for many years.
They also used them as tools for moving the giant moai
. Eventually every single tree on the entire island was
gone! Without trees the soil suffered from severe erosion and became depleted of its
nutrients. Farming the land became difficult. I asked Mr. Fay why the Rapanui didn't
leave. He said they probably couldn't. To leave, they would have needed canoes. And what do you need to make canoes? Yep, you got it—trees!
The story of Easter Island shows us just how important it is to take care of the environment and use natural resources wisely.
I was really glad to learn that new trees are now being planted on Easter Island.
Maybe someday palm trees will cover the island again, just as they did when the Rapanui first arrived.
After our landmarks lesson, we got to make our own moai out of clay. I made mine standing on a platform.
It looked a little sad all by itself, so I added something else: a tall, leafy palm tree!
See you next week!
Hey, Little Fox readers. It's me, Alex, again. I took a trip to New York City with my family recently, and we went to the top of the Empire State building.
When it was built more than 75 years ago, it was the tallest building in the world.
But Mr. Fay just told us about another cool skyscraper—one that's more than twice that tall.
It's the Burj Khalifa, located in Dubai. And as of 2010, it was the tallest building in the whole world!
Dubai is a city in the United Arab Emirates, a small country on the Persian Gulf in the Middle East.
Years ago people went to Dubai mainly to fish or dive for pearls.
But after oil was discovered there in 1966, the city had a massive construction boom.
And now it's a bustling world financial center, with tourists flocking to its upscale restaurants, stores, and hotels.
Dubai also has some amazing sights, like man-made islands shaped like a map of the world and a ski resort that's indoors.
Plus, Mr. Fay said there are plans to construct even more unique buildings, including a skyscraper with rotating floors and the world's first underwater hotel. I'd sure like to stay there!
But for now the Burj Khalifa is one of the most impressive buildings in Dubai.
It was designed by Adrian Smith, a well-known architect, and an engineer named William F. Baker.
They wanted the building to reflect modern architecture as well as the region's natural beauty.
So to represent the Hymenocallis , a local flower, there are three wings arranged around a central
core. The wings are set at different heights and appear to spiral around the
building. This unique design makes for fantastic views of the Persian
Gulf. More importantly, it helps to reduce the effects of Dubai's strong desert winds, which can reach speeds of fifty kilometers per hour near the
ground. And at the top of the building, the wind can be about three times that
strong! Since Dubai sits on a geological fault line, the building's designers faced another challenge: they had to make the tower strong enough to withstand
earthquakes. That's why the building's three sections are buttressed by special concrete
walls. These walls, along with the enormous concrete column in the center of the tower, make the building very
sturdy. Oh, and Mr. Fay told us something really
surprising. Since cities sometimes try to outdo each other by building taller and taller skyscrapers, the developers of the Burj Khalifa decided to keep their tower's final height a
secret. But while they were building it, everyone could see that it was going to be one very tall
building. The construction of the Burj Khalifa took about six years.
During the peak of construction, there were more than twelve thousand workers at the site every single day!
The building officially opened in January 2010 with a huge celebration and a massive fireworks display.
At the grand opening, the builders finally revealed the exact height of the giant silver tower—828 meters—making it the tallest freestanding structure in the world.
We learned some other really cool facts about the Burj Khalifa from Mr. Fay.
It has 57 elevators, 8 escalators, and about 160 floors that are used as offices and apartments.
There's also a really fancy restaurant and an expensive hotel that was designed by a famous fashion designer.
The building also has about 28,000 glass panels.
When I asked Mr. Fay how they get washed, he explained that workers have to be harnessed into special mechanical units that extend out from the sides of the building.
It takes three to four months to clean all that glass.
Can you imagine washing windows up that high? I get dizzy just thinking about it!
Speaking of heights, on the 124th floor of the Burj Khalifa, there's an observation deck.
It's called At the Top, and it has floor-to-ceiling windows with amazing views of the city, the surrounding desert, and the Persian Gulf.
And if you're feeling brave while you're up that high, you can check out the world's highest outdoor observation deck. Yikes!
Mr. Fay told us that the world's tallest building isn't the only thing to see in the area.
The Dubai Mall is nearby, and since this is Dubai we're talking about, the mall isn't just big; it's the biggest mall in the whole world.
In addition to plenty of expensive stores, it has an aquarium, an Olympic-sized ice rink, and an indoor amusement park.
The mall is also where you start your trip to At the Top.
A moving walkway transports you from the mall to the high-speed elevators inside the Burj Khalifa.
Lots of people also enjoy spending time at the park nearby.
There's a lake, a promenade, a small forest, and a huge fountain with 1,500 jets that spray water over 150 meters high.
With music, fog machines, and over six thousand lights, this famous "performing fountain" puts on quite a show!
After the landmarks lesson, Mr. Fay gave our class a special assignment: we had to work with a partner and design our own skyscraper.
Jake and I had lots of fun making ours. We used cardboard and covered it with aluminum foil to make our building shiny, like the Burj Khalifa.
But we decided to put only one thing inside our tall tower—a gigantic water slide! Awesome, huh?
Hi, everyone. Our class just finished watching a documentary about the Dead Sea.
We learned a lot of cool stuff about it. Did you know that people go there just to smear mud all over themselves? I’ll tell you more about that in a minute!
The Dead Sea, in case you don't know, is actually a lake in the Middle East.
At four hundred meters below sea level, it's the lowest point on Earth.
But we found out that it's mostly famous for all the salt and minerals it contains.
The water in the Dead Sea is almost six times saltier than ocean water!
The Dead Sea lies between the borders of Jordan, Israel, and the West Bank.
It’s about 80 kilometers long, 11 kilometers wide at its widest point, and 377 meters deep at its deepest.
The lake is surrounded by hot, dry desert on all sides, and it's located in an area known as the Dead Sea Depression.
I didn't know what a depression was until Mr. Fay explained that it's a low-lying area caused by something called a rift.
A rift occurs when two plates of the earth's crust move apart.
The land between them gets stretched thinner and thinner. And as the land gets thinner, it sinks, creating a depression.
Maybe you're wondering, just like I was, how the Dead Sea got so salty.
Well, the depression sits so low that water from all the nearby rivers drains into it. This water is filled with salt and minerals.
And since the depression is lower than all the surrounding land, the water can never drain back out; it can only evaporate.
And that's what happens—water constantly evaporates.
In fact, so much water is evaporating from the Dead Sea, it often looks like there's a cloud of fog hanging over the lake.
(That's pretty creepy when you think about the Dead Sea's name, huh?)
Anyway, as the water evaporates, it leaves behind the salt and minerals.
Now I can tell you why people go to the Dead Sea to cover themselves from head to toe with its mud!
All the minerals that get deposited into the lake sink down into the mud at the bottom.
And those minerals are supposed to be really good for your skin.
No wonder lots of spas and health resorts have been built in the area.
After hearing so much about the Dead Sea's health benefits, I wanted to know why it has such a grim name.
According to the documentary we watched in class, the water in the Dead Sea is so salty that almost nothing can live there, except for bacteria and one type of algae.
Any fish or freshwater animal that gets washed into the lake dies almost instantly.
And the shores are covered in thick salt crystals, so animals can’t even survive near the lake either.
But don’t worry; the water is totally safe for people.
You can even go swimming there if you want, although it's pretty hard to swim because all that salt makes it much easier to float!
In fact, that movie showed people sitting up and reading in the Dead Sea, as if they were sitting in chairs. It was unbelievable!
The Dead Sea also has an important place in history. It's mentioned in the Bible, and there are stories about Queen Cleopatra traveling to the lake to bathe.
It's also where the Dead Sea Scrolls were discovered.
These ancient manuscripts, which were made from papyrus, leather, and copper, were found in 1947 in caves near the lake’s shore.
They're the oldest known copies of the Old Testament, dating all the way back to the third and first centuries BC.
Unfortunately, like many other beautiful and historic places in the world, the Dead Sea's existence is threatened.
Over the last thirty years or so, its water level has dropped by nearly one meter a year, and it has lost almost a third of its surface area.
This is because the waters of its main source—the Jordan River—are being diverted.
The countries of Israel, Syria, and Jordan are diverting fresh water from the Jordan River in order to farm and provide drinking water to people living in cities.
Israel and Jordan also deliberately evaporate large pools of water just to extract the Dead Sea's minerals.
The scientists in the movie think the depression itself is sinking every year too.
Some scientists think the rift is the cause. Others believe that the sinking is due to changes in the ground's composition.
Either way the lake is reported to sink about 33 centimeters every year!
Sadly Mr. Fay said that the countries around the Dead Sea don't have the greatest relations right now.
That makes it very difficult for environmentalists to come together and try to help the Jordan River and the Dead Sea.
But I hope they do. I want to try floating there someday!
After we watched the movie about the Dead Sea, Alex and I came up with a great idea for a project:
our class can write letters to environmental protection groups asking them to support the conservation of the Jordan River.
This will help to save the "dying" Dead Sea.
The movie definitely gave me a lot of facts for my letter.
But I still have more research to do, so I'd better go now. See you next time!
Hey, Little Fox Readers. It's me, Jake, and I'm pretty excited to tell you about this week's landmark—the Sagrada Familia in Barcelona, Spain.
That's because this huge Catholic cathedral is different from all the other landmarks we've studied so far: it's still being built!
In fact, it won't be completed until around 2026. By then it will have taken over 140 years to build!
The idea for the Sagrada Familia was born back in 1872 when a Spanish bookseller named Josep Maria Bocabella saw a beautiful church in Italy and dreamed of building a similar one in Barcelona.
With the help of a society he'd founded earlier, Bocabella was able to begin construction on the Sagrada Familia by 1882.
Over the years many different architects have overseen the construction of the Sagrada Familia.
Most of these people have stayed close to the original design created by Antoni Gaudi, who was hired as the cathedral's main architect in 1883.
In the beginning Gaudi worked on other buildings too, but from 1914 on, he devoted all his time to the Sagrada Familia.
He became so devoted that he practically moved into his workshop inside the cathedral for the last few months of his life.
I guess all that hard work paid off because today the Sagrada Familia is known as Gaudi's masterpiece!
On June 10, 1926, Gaudi died in a tragic accident: while walking to a church service, he was run over by a street tram.
He was buried in the Sagrada Familia's crypt, which had been finished by then.
Fortunately Gaudi had known all along that the cathedral couldn't be completed during his lifetime, so he'd been thinking of ways to allow the project to continue even after his death.
For example, he planned the construction in stages to make it easier for the generations of builders after him.
He also spent a lot of time making models and drawing detailed plans of everything.
The Sagrada Familia is a Catholic house of worship, but it can also be seen as a monument to nature.
The main hall of the church, called the central nave, was designed to make visitors feel like they are standing under a glowing forest canopy.
Huge, tree-like columns rise to a double roof, which reflects natural light.
Also the gates, walls, and floors are covered with intricate patterns that look like honeycombs, palm leaves, and vines.
Oh, and check out my favorite detail—spiral stairways that are modeled after snail shells!
The outside of the building imitates nature too. The towers are made of shapes that resemble minerals and plants that can be found near Barcelona.
And if you look carefully at one of the building's sides, you can see detailed sculptures of almost two hundred different species of plants and animals.
Over the years people have had mixed reactions toward Gaudi's one-of-a-kind design.
Some people have praised it as brilliant and imaginative while others have described it as bizarre or hideous.
The famous British author George Orwell called it one of the ugliest buildings in the world!
Personally, I think it looks pretty cool—like something from a fantasy movie. What do you think?
The Sagrada Familia has been called a Bible in stone because the building's carvings, sculptures, and structures represent Catholic beliefs and stories.
I think the best examples of these stories are the building's three sides, also called facades.
The Nativity facade is the one with all the sculptures of plants and animals.
It faces east, where the sun rises, to symbolize the birth of Jesus.
The Passion facade was built with sad, dramatic sculptures and bone-shaped columns to symbolize the suffering and death of Jesus.
It faces west, becoming shadowy and eerie as the sun sets. Gaudi actually hoped that this facade would scare people!
While the Passion facade represents darkness and shadow, the Glory facade symbolizes eternal light and joy.
It faces south, receiving lots of sunlight, to celebrate the resurrection of Jesus.
Its construction began around 2000, and it will be the last facade to be completed.
Once it's finished, it will serve as the main entrance to the Sagrada Familia.
The cathedral will also have a total of 18 towers that symbolize important Christian figures such as the Virgin Mary and the apostles.

The central tower, dedicated to Jesus, will be illuminated at night by the surrounding towers and will stretch an amazing 170 meters into the sky, making the Sagrada Familia the tallest cathedral in the world!
Today over two million visitors come to Barcelona each year to see the cathedral.
Tourists can take a trip down to the crypt or up to the towers, walk around the central nave, or explore some of the exhibitions on display, including a replica of Gaudi's workshop.
Tourists also get to play an important role: the money they pay to visit the Sagrada Familia goes toward finishing it because it's an expiatory church.
That means most of its funding comes from private donations and contributions—from wealthy people and organizations, as well as ordinary people like you and me!
After the lesson about the Sagrada Familia, I thought it would be really neat if our class could send a donation too.
To raise money, we sold cookies, brownies, and cupcakes after school.
Mr. Fay told all the other classes to come and help support the Sagrada Familia, and our bake sale was a huge success!
This week was awesome. Our class not only got to study a world landmark, we got to help build one too.
And remember, the Sagrada Familia isn't finished yet, so it's not too late for you to help too!
Hi there, Little Fox readers! Have you ever heard of penguins living near the equator or seen birds with bright blue feet?
Did you know that some animals can live to be 150 years old?
Well, in this week's landmarks lesson, we learned about the Galapagos Islands, which are famous for all the really unusual animals that live there!
The Galapagos Islands are located on the equator, about one thousand kilometers west of mainland South America.
This archipelago, or group of islands, consists of 13 big islands, 6 smaller ones, and a whole bunch of tiny ones.
Scientists believe that the islands were formed millions of years ago by eruptions from underwater volcanoes.
The islands' shores are barren and rocky, but there's plenty of vegetation inland. Some areas are covered with huge cacti that look like trees.
There are also dense forests and humid swamps that create enough fog to completely hide the islands sometimes.
Mr. Fay said that's probably why the Galapagos Islands were a popular hideout for British pirates in the seventeenth century.
Nobody actually lived on the islands, so after attacking Spanish ships or settlements, the pirates would retreat to them.
With all that thick fog, the pirates couldn't be spotted by people aboard passing ships!
Alex and Jake thought the stories about the pirates were really cool.
But if you ask me, the most interesting thing about the Galapagos Islands is the wildlife that lives there.
Many of the animal species are endemic, which means you won't find them anywhere else in the world.
Not only that, most of these species vary from one island to another.
When the naturalist Charles Darwin visited the Galapagos Islands in 1835, he was amazed by how unique and diverse the animals on the islands are.
Darwin noticed, for example, that each island has its own distinct species of finch, with its own unique beak shape and size.
One finch species is even smarter than the others—it uses tools!
But it doesn't use power saws or hammers or anything; this finch uses sticks to dig for bugs. Pretty incredible, huh?
Anyway, Darwin's observations about the finches and other animals on the Galapagos Islands eventually inspired his famous theories about natural selection.
Many other kinds of birds live on the Galapagos Islands too.
The blue-footed booby is my favorite because it has bright blue feet and looks very fashionable!
Mr. Fay also told us about a strange bird called the magnificent frigate bird. The male has a huge red pouch under its beak.
And get this: the magnificent frigate bird can't take off from flat ground—it has to run down a hill to build up enough speed! How weird is that?
There's also one type of bird you'd never expect to see living so close to the equator—the Galapagos penguin. But it's not easy for them to survive there.
These penguins are threatened whenever the temperature of the water rises by even a few degrees. The
most famous animal on the Galapagos Islands is probably the Galapagos giant tortoise. In
fact, the islands are named after these tortoises; the Spanish word for "tortoise" is galapago .
These big reptiles can grow to be over 1.5 meters long and weigh up to 250 kilograms.
They can also go a whole year without eating or drinking anything. But that's nothing compared to how long they can live—150 years!
Another fascinating reptile on the islands is the marine iguana. Usually iguanas stay on land.
But scientists believe that when food became scarce, some Galapagos iguanas started hunting in the water.
Over many generations these iguanas evolved into great swimmers.
The marine iguanas can swim about fifteen meters deep and stay underwater for almost a half an hour.
It's the only lizard in the world that swims in the ocean, and it can only be found on the Galapagos Islands.
As you've probably figured out by now, the Galapagos Islands are a pretty important and unique landmark that's worth preserving.
Luckily the islands were turned into a national park in 1959. Even the waters surrounding the islands are protected as a reserve.
A big threat to the Galapagos Islands today is tourism. Over 100,000 people visit the archipelago each year, threatening its fragile ecosystems.

Scientists at the Charles Darwin Research Station, which was also established in 1959, study the islands' plant and animal life and work closely with the Galapagos National Park Service to protect the area.
Tourists have to follow trails, and park workers carefully monitor the number of people allowed on the islands.
Park workers also make sure that tour guides are properly licensed so that rules and regulations are strictly followed.
Tourists can't touch the animals or remove anything from the islands.
If you go, though, you'll probably be able to get very close to some of the animals.
Since the islands were uninhabited by people until recently (except for those pirates, of course!), many of the animals are not afraid of humans and will let you walk right up to them.
Mr. Fay showed us a picture of a person sitting in front of a sea lion on the beach!
There are also plenty of animals to see in the water. Divers around the islands can swim alongside fish, sharks, morays, and even whales.
I don't know about you, but I think it would be totally amazing to swim alongside a huge whale shark.
After the landmarks lesson, Mr. Fay gave us a fun assignment: we have to write a report on our favorite Galapagos animal.
I picked the blue-footed booby, of course. So I started doing a little research, and guess what I found out. There's also a red-footed booby!
Hmm . . . blue feet or red feet. Now I can't decide which one I like better!
Hi, everyone. I'm trying to find a place to hide this pretty emerald ring that my uncle gave me for my birthday. My brother keeps trying to steal it from me!
I like the ring because it reminds me of an awesome landmark in Myanmar that Mr. Fay told us about.
It's called the Shwedagon Pagoda, but I like to think of it as the Tower of Sparkling Jewels!
It's not just a giant golden building; it's holy too. The Shwedagon Pagoda is actually a Buddhist shrine that's over 2,500 years old.
What makes it so holy? Get this—it holds some of the Buddha's actual hair!
First let me give you a picture of what the pagoda looks like, so you can see why everyone makes such a big deal about it.
This landmark is really a complex of temples that sits high upon a hill in Yangon, the old capital city of Myanmar.
The main pagoda is about one hundred meters tall and shaped like a giant cone.
Its name, Shwedagon, means something like "golden place" because it's literally covered in gold and jewels.
The main pagoda has ten sections or layers. The base of the pagoda is covered with 8,688 solid gold blocks.
Above that are three terraces used by monks for worship and prayer.
On top of them is a bell-shaped section, followed by something that looks like an upside-down bowl with golden bands above it.
Above that are lotus petals. Whew! And there's still more—all of that is topped by a bud-shaped spire and a crown!
Considered the main jewel piece, the crown is covered with 5,448 diamonds plus 2,317 other jewels like rubies and sapphires.
In the center of this sparkling display is a giant emerald that reflects light at sunrise and sunset. I bet that's beautiful to see!
Then there's a flag-shaped vane that reaches toward the sky and supports the final diamond bud at the top—a glittering 76-karat diamond.
During the day the pagoda shines in the sun, and at night, it sparkles in the lights that illuminate the complex.
The pagoda has over forty different halls and shrines, and it's filled with statues of buddhas and mythical creatures, bodhi trees, and beautiful flowers.
It is also surrounded by 64 smaller pagodas.
I think you could spend all day exploring the place.
Oh! And there are even two "wishing" buddha statues in the pagoda, where you can go to make a wish!
I wonder what I would wish for . . . maybe a new little brother. Just kidding!
Even though the pagoda looks amazing from the outside, it's not just a tourist spectacle.
It's still a functioning temple with resident monks who meditate and pray all day long.
And since the pagoda is a sacred place, all visitors, even those who are just there to tour the grounds, have to wear modest clothing and remove their shoes before entering.
When Mr. Fay went, he did what most people do when they arrive at Shwedagon.
He walked clockwise around the octagonal base of the pagoda to see the statues of buddhas where visitors leave offerings of flowers and incense.
Next Mr. Fay went up one of the four main stairwells that lead into the pagoda.
Each stairwell has over one hundred steps, so you need to be determined—and in shape—to reach the top!
Mr. Fay climbed the southern stairway, which is lined with little shops selling books, charms, colorful prayer flags, and other things.
He even bought a small statue of the pagoda for our classroom!
You're probably wondering why the pagoda was built in the first place. Well, it's a great story that is part legend and part history.
Legend has it that Singuttara Hill has always been a holy place because relics of three past buddhas were buried there thousands and thousands of years ago.
Around 580 BC a king named Okkalapa knew that in order to keep Singuttara Hill holy, relics of a buddha needed to be enshrined there again.
So he sat on the hill and prayed and meditated for new relics to be brought to his kingdom.
At the same time, Siddhartha Gautama of India, also known as Lord Buddha, was meditating on his path to enlightenment.
Coincidentally, two of King Okkalapa's subjects were out walking when they came upon Lord Buddha meditating.
They offered him food, and in return Lord Buddha gave them eight hairs from his head.
The two subjects rushed back to their kingdom to offer the hairs to King Okkalapa.
The king was overjoyed and built a pagoda to enshrine these holy relics. This became the original Shwedagon Pagoda.
Over the years the pagoda has been rebuilt and expanded, and kings and queens from around Asia have donated a countless number of jewels and gold.
Today the pagoda attracts thousands of Buddhist pilgrims and tourists each year.
Unfortunately the history of the pagoda includes some disasters too.
There was a terrible fire there in 1931, and the city of Yangon has experienced at least eight massive earthquakes, a tidal wave, fighting during World War II, and occupation by foreign countries.
But the Shwedagon Pagoda has miraculously survived all this and been rebuilt more beautifully each time.
According to Buddhist tradition, pagodas generate peace and promote loving kindness in the land where they are built.
So the Shwedagon Pagoda is really a magical place, and I hope it survives any other disasters that may come its way!
In the meantime I need to find a place to hide this ring before my brother gets home from school.
Maybe I'll just keep it in my pocket and hold it up to the sunlight each sunrise and sunset, so it can sparkle just like the emerald at the Shwedagon Pagoda.
Oh no . . . Here comes my brother. I've got to go now! See you next time!
Hola, amigos ! That's Spanish for "Hello, friends!" I'm learning Spanish because—get this—my parents might let me study abroad in Spain this
summer! And it's all thanks to Mr. Fay. He told us about a landmark there that sounds so cool, I want to check it
out. It's a medieval fortress and complex of palaces called the
Alhambra. The word alhambra means "the red" in
Arabic. The complex was named that because the entire place is surrounded by walls made of red gravel and clay
bricks. From the outside the Alhambra looks pretty plain, but on the inside, everything is decorated with fancy tiles and
carvings. Oh, and here's a cool fact: the walls are covered with calligraphy because the original builders were actually ordered to write all over
them! So why does a place in Spain have an Arabic name? Mr. Fay had to give us a little history first so we could understand
that. In the 700s Arab Muslims invaded and took over large parts of
Spain. For the next 700 years or so, Spain was a battleground for Christians and these Muslims, known as
Moors. Eventually, in 1492, Catholic monarchs regained control and ousted the Moors from their
kingdom. But the Moors left their mark with the Alhambra, a beautiful walled city they’d built in
Granada. Years before, when the Moors were fighting Christian armies, the rulers had needed a military fortress that would be naturally
protected. On a rocky hill in southern Spain, they found an old fort from the eighth
century. The hill was near a river, so there was access to water, and the area was protected by mountains and
woods. It was the ideal place to put their lookout tower and royal
residence. Over time Moorish rulers continued to expand the Alhambra; construction began during the ninth century and continued through the late fifteenth
century. At its peak the complex contained a military fortress, two palaces and courts, artisan workshops, baths, and a
mosque. The oldest remaining section of the complex is the military area, known as the
Alcazaba. It contains several towers, including the original watchtower, which is about 27 meters
tall. After climbing the steep, narrow staircase to the top, royal guards could watch for invaders and even attack enemies from
above. I bet it felt like the top of the world up
there! The Alcazaba also had military barracks, secret passageways, and even underground dungeons for
prisoners! Another section of the Alhambra is a great hall known as the
Mexuar. Remember how I said there was lots of writing on the
walls? Well, Islamic law forbids the drawing or painting of living things, so all the decorations in the Alhambra had to be geometric designs or
calligraphy. I think it was a really smart idea to write on the
walls. For example, at the door to the Mexuar, it says, "Enter and
ask. Do not be afraid to seek justice for here you will find it."
And guess what went on there? That's right—official government business, including all matters of justice and the law.
It was where the sultan and government officials held meetings and public forums for people to voice complaints.
The fanciest parts of the Alhambra are the palaces, of course.
Two were built during the Arab rule, and a third was commissioned later by a Christian king in the 1500s.
The two Arab palaces are the Comares Palace and the Palace of the Lions.
The Comares Palace was the official royal residence, built between 1333 and 1370.
The sultan lived there with his wives and guards.
From the pictures Mr. Fay showed us, it sure looks like a sultan's home!
The palace is centered around a courtyard that has a long pool fed by two fountains.
Green myrtle bushes line the pool, giving the courtyard its name—the Court of Myrtle.
In the right light, the water reflects the bushes' color, making the edges of the pool look green.
The courtyard also has a white marble patio with intricately decorated arches and columns.
Historians think the Alhambra was built primarily to show the greatness of Allah, or God.
Every sight within the complex was supposed to remind people of the beauty of Allah's creation.
The Palace of the Lions, another royal residence, was built between 1362 and 1391.
Its courtyard has a magnificent fountain supported by twelve lions spouting water—the only representations of living forms in the Alhambra.
The courtyard is supported by white marble columns, and its ceilings are decorated with carved, lace-like designs, and fancy calligraphy.
I can't even imagine how long it must have taken to carve all that by hand!
In 1527 the Christian king, Charles V, decided that he liked the Alhambra so much, he wanted to build himself a summer palace there.
He planned for it to be bigger and better than the Arab palaces, and built in a Christian style.
But unfortunately for Charles V, the construction wasn't completed until 1957 because he ran out of money. Oops!
Today the Alhambra is the only remaining palace complex that can show us the beauty of medieval Muslim design and architecture.
Sadly it no longer looks exactly like it did during the Middle Ages and the Renaissance.
