After 1492 Christian monarchs regained control of Spain and destroyed sections of the Alhambra, rebuilding them in European Renaissance style.
The Alhambra has since faced fires, earthquakes, gunpowder explosions, and wreckage caused by tourists.
As recently as fifty years ago, visitors were carving their names into the walls and chipping off pieces of tiles as souvenirs!
Luckily in 1984 the Alhambra was named a World Heritage site, so it's now strictly preserved.
Well, I’d better keep practicing my Spanish. My parents said I can only go to Spain if I speak nothing but Spanish to them until June.
And a trip filled with medieval castles sounds too fun to pass up! See you next time!
Hi, everybody. I only have a few minutes to talk because Alex and Melissa are about to come over.
We're working on a project for Mr. Fay's class, where we just learned about the Serengeti, a savanna plain in eastern Africa.
Our assignment is to make a poster advertising a safari tour.
We have to include interesting things about the Serengeti that will make people want to go on this tour.
We learned tons of cool things in class, but here's my favorite: every year, for the past two million years or so, the Serengeti hosts one of the largest migrations on earth.
Over a million wildebeests stampede over the grassy plains in search of water and food!
Did you know that humans have lived in the Serengeti for over two million years too?
Mr. Fay told us that the landscapes, animals, and climate of the Serengeti haven't really changed much in all these years.
So if you visit today, you can easily imagine what it looked like a million years ago.
The Serengeti covers nearly thirty thousand square kilometers and contains a variety of landscapes.
It is most famous for its endless grassy plains, which seem to go on and on forever. But there are also rivers, forests, and volcanoes.
Let me tell you about the wildebeests' migration, since that will be the main feature of our poster.
The wildebeests live in the volcanic plains of the southern Serengeti from December to June, which is the rainy season.
They need water to drink and food to eat, which are plentiful, as long as there's rain.
But after June the southern Serengeti becomes desert-like as the hot sun dries up the soil.
So the wildebeests—nearly two million of them—travel west, then north, then south in search of rain until they come back, full circle, a year later.
So how do they know where to go? Well, scientists have figured out that wildebeests can detect rain from up to fifty kilometers away.
But nobody knows exactly how they do this.
Scientists do know that the wildebeests are a crucial part of the Serengeti's ecosystem.
During their migration the animals act as natural lawn mowers and fertilizers by eating grass, digging up soil with their stampeding hooves, and then depositing their waste.
Mr. Fay described their waste as a daily present to the Earth.
And guess how much that daily present weighs? 420 tons! That is a lot of dung!
The wildebeests are awesome, but no tour of the Serengeti would be complete without the "Big Five."
These are the five animals that are so dangerous, they've been known since ancient times as the beasts that hunt the hunters: lions, leopards, rhinos, buffalo, and elephants.
The Big Five are huge animals that don't like humans interfering with their habitat.
If you ever visit the Serengeti, be prepared to wake up to the frightening roar of leopards or the grunt of an angry buffalo outside your tent!
And you should definitely know what to do if you see a 5,000-kilogram elephant flapping its ears at you.
Run and climb the nearest tree because that means the elephant is about to charge!
So you might be wondering how humans could possibly live in a place like the Serengeti.
Well, the Maasai people have been living in the Serengeti for years.
Now they are mostly cattle herdsmen, who sometimes roam with their herds to find food and water.
According to a Maasai saying, cattle and children are the most important things to Maasai people.
Even today many Maasai still live in traditional houses made of mud, grass, sticks, and cow dung.
And guess who builds these houses? Women!
The men are in charge of herding and protecting while the women's duties are house-building and cooking.
I can't wait to hear what my mom thinks about that.
In class Mr. Fay showed us lots of pictures of the Maasai, and I thought they looked cool in their red robes and colorful beads.
Beaded jewelry is a symbol of age and status, and red is a symbol of courage in Maasai culture.
They sound like some of the most courageous people on earth, living out there with the Big Five, forever ready to protect their cattle.
But the Maasai way of life is slowly becoming threatened as more land in the Serengeti is preserved and grazing areas become restricted.
When national parks were created there to preserve game and wildlife, the Maasai were kicked off land they had roamed for years.
Mr. Fay says it's tough to balance the need to protect natural resources and wildlife with the need to allow people to make a living.
Poverty in Africa and a high demand for wild meat have caused poachers, or illegal hunters, to venture into the protected parks of the Serengeti to hunt.
Officials say about forty thousand to two hundred thousand animals are killed every year by poachers.
This makes conservationists, who are trying to protect endangered species there, distraught. Hearing this made me pretty mad too.
One way people try to preserve this balance of economy and ecology is by offering safari tours.
Guiding these tours provides locals with an income that doesn't come from harming the land. And it's a big business!
About ninety thousand tourists a year visit the Serengeti to "go on a safari," or ride in protected vehicles, hoping to catch glimpses of hunting lions, migrating wildebeests, and grazing gazelles.
Even if you're not adventurous enough to go on a safari, you can still have a good time viewing birds, visiting national parks, and taking amazing photos.
It sounds like Melissa and Alex are here, so I'd better go now.
We're planning to work on our poster outside; that way it won't get too messy in here.
But first I've got a question for you: now that you've learned all these cool things about the Serengeti, would you go on our tour?
Hi there, Little Fox readers. Sorry I'm in a bad mood today. But it's a really nice day, and my parents are making me go to a boring play at a stuffy old theater.
My mom says it'll be fun, but I'd much rather be outside with my friends.
Oh! That reminds me of our latest landmarks lesson! We just learned about a very famous outdoor theater—the Colosseum.
Completed around 80 AD, this ancient amphitheater is a symbol of the once mighty Roman Empire.
It's also the largest amphitheater ever erected in Rome—with enough seats to hold over fifty thousand spectators!
Construction of the Colosseum began around 70 AD during the reign of the emperor Vespasian.
Vespasian had come to power after Nero, a cruel emperor who executed lots of people and plunged the empire into chaos.
Determined to restore order to Rome and pride to its citizens, Vespasian launched many public works projects.
One of these projects was the construction of a magnificent arena in the center of the city, on land that Nero had once seized from the people.
Following Vespasian's orders, teams of professional architects, engineers, and decorators designed the building, with about 100,000 slaves providing the manual labor.
And because the ancient Romans had recently invented an inexpensive new building material—concrete—the new arena could be built cheaply, and pretty quickly too.
Shaped like an oval (which is still the shape of most outdoor arenas today), the Colosseum had four tiers of seats.
Workers created eighty entrance arches, so that big crowds could quickly flow in and out.
The building was decorated with fountains and painted statues and even had soft cushions resting on its seats!
Mr. Fay also showed us pictures of an incredible network of underground rooms.
These were mostly used for storing supplies and props for the shows, including exotic animals like lions, rhinos, and—yikes!—crocodiles!
The city celebrated the opening of the Colosseum with one hundred days of games and festivities.
At first it was called the Flavian Amphitheater to honor Vespasian's family, the Flavian dynasty.
But over time the building became known as the Colosseum because of the enormous, or colossal, statue of Nero that had once stood there.
The Colosseum is pretty famous for its tall, decorative columns, which inspired many other architectural works around the world.
But if you ask me, the coolest thing about the building is its amazing engineering.
Roman builders created lots of different machines to help shows run smoothly and keep the crowds comfortable; many of these devices are still used in theaters and arenas today.
There were elevators and pulleys to lift equipment and props.
Trapdoors opened under the floor for special effects, and on hot days, a special awning could be stretched over the building to block the sun.
Engineers even designed a system for flooding the arena so that mock sea battles could be staged!
It sounds like those ancient builders thought of everything, doesn't it?
Admission to events at the Colosseum was free, but spectators still needed tickets for seating.
And people had to sit in sections based on their social rank:
Rome's wealthiest citizens got to sit in the first tier while poor Romans and women were stuck sitting far from the action, way up at the very top.
By now you're probably wondering what kinds of shows they had at the Colosseum. Well . . . I hate to tell you this, but most of them were pretty bloody.
Mr. Fay said that as many as 700,000 people may have died there, along with even more animals.
Sometimes so much blood was spilled, the sand covering the floor turned red.
Most of the people who died at the Colosseum were gladiators—professional fighters who battled to the death to entertain Roman audiences.
Some gladiators volunteered to fight while others, like slaves, were forced to fight.
The sport was so popular in ancient Rome, there were even special gladiator schools!
Other events at the Colosseum included animal hunts and exhibits as well as dramas based on mythology.
People used to believe that Christians were martyred there, fed to lions because of their religious beliefs.
But today most historians say this is just a legend. I sure hope they're right.
Fortunately, the violent contests between gladiators were outlawed around 400 AD.
In 523 AD the animal hunts and games were put to a stop too. With the end of the games, the Colosseum fell into disrepair.
In the years that followed, it was turned into a cemetery, a fortress, and a site for religious events.
Its grounds were constantly looted; people carried off stones, as well as gold and bronze objects.
Today the Colosseum is one of the most popular tourist sites in the world, with millions of visitors each year.
Although it's in ruins from all the looting, and damaged from air pollution and earthquakes, you can still see the outer shell of the building.
You can also peek at the underground rooms and imagine what it was like when huge beasts and powerful gladiators prowled through those ancient corridors.
In 2011 a restoration project was begun to help preserve the Colosseum.
Like Mr. Fay said, it's important to remember the terrible violence that happened there.
Still the Colosseum is a remarkable example of Roman architecture and human achievement.
The famous writer Charles Dickens once described it like this:
"It is the most impressive, the most stately, the most solemn, grand, majestic, mournful sight, conceivable."
You know what? After telling you about the Colosseum, I feel a little better about going to the play today.
The show might be boring, but at least it won't be violent and bloody like those gladiator battles!
Hey, everybody. I'm back to tell you about another landmark. But first check out this rainbow.
Isn't it cool? It appeared right after the thunderstorm we just had!
The rainbow in my backyard is amazing, but it's not as awesome as the ones that appear at Victoria Falls, the landmark Mr. Fay taught us about today.
Victoria Falls is right on the border of Zimbabwe and Zambia in southern Africa.
It's where the giant Zambezi River falls suddenly into a deep gorge, creating the world's largest curtain of falling water.
Mr. Fay said Victoria Falls is one of the Seven Natural Wonders of the World!
According to geologists, the Zambezi River has been sculpting the plains of Africa for about two million years.
The incredible force of this 3,540-kilometer river cuts through weak areas of rock, creating cracks and gorges.
Today the river tumbles from the edge of a grassy plain into a gorge, forming Victoria Falls.
The gorge is only about 25 to 75 meters wide; if it weren't for the spray from the falls, from far away it might look like the water was just disappearing into the earth!
The African name for the falls is Mosi-oa-Tunya , which means the "The Smoke that
Thunders." If you ever visit this place, you'll easily see why it's named
that. The spray from the falls—which can rise four hundred to eight hundred meters during the flood season—looks like smoke billowing up into the
sky. It can be seen from up to twenty kilometers
away! And the roar . . . Well, let me tell you about the
roar. Millions of liters of water crashing from a height of 108 meters sounds like thunder booming from about twenty storms at
once! The odd thing is that Victoria Falls is in a part of Africa that experiences both wet and dry seasons. The wet season peaks around February or
March. This is when you can see the 1,700-meter-wide curtain of water and its magnificent
sprays. But during the dry season, from around May to November, the huge curtain disappears, and Victoria Falls turns into a series of small
waterfalls. Mr. Fay told us that a lot of tourists have a hard time deciding when to
visit. In the wet season, the powerful falls are awesome, but the spray is so high and thick you can hardly see
anything! Some people choose to go in the dry season because the smaller waterfalls are still pretty, and the lower water levels reveal little islands that are upstream from the
falls. You can even take boat tours to these islands and get an incredible view of the water as it disappears over the
edge! One of these islands, Livingstone Island, is named for the Scottish explorer Dr. David
Livingstone. In the 1850s Livingstone and his team were exploring the area around the Zambezi River when some locals told him that he must view the "Smoke That Thunders."
In 1855 he became the first European to ever see the natural wonder, and he named it Victoria Falls, after Queen Victoria.
Apparently he was stunned by the beauty of what he saw.

In his travel journals, he wrote, "The whole scene was extremely beautiful; the banks and islands dotted over the river are adorned with . . . great variety of color and form . . . no one can imagine the beauty of the view . . ."
And in his description of the water itself he wrote, "The snow-white sheet seemed like . . . small comets rushing on in one direction, each of which left behind its . . . rays of foam."
Today there is a monument on Livingstone Island commemorating Dr. Livingstone, but what really draws tourists to the island is its closeness to Devil's Pool.
Adventure-seekers can jump into the small but deep pool that sits right at the crest of the falls.
From there you can look down over the falls while actually standing in the river.
But if you're not a good swimmer, or the water is too high, you could get swept away and tumble down into the rocky gorge!
So just for fun, let's pretend that you somehow manage to survive the hundred- meter drop into the gorge.
After the long plunge, you'd end up in the Boiling Pot, a deep pool at the end of the gorge, along with the remains of hippos and zebras that have gotten carried off by the river during floods.
But don't worry; the water in the Boiling Pot isn't really boiling.
It just churns and foams, so it looks as if it's boiling.
If you manage to flow free from the Boiling Pot, you'd end up traveling along the Zambezi River through Mozambique, all the way out to the Indian Ocean.
There are many other ways to enjoy the falls.
You can take a helicopter tour or fly over the river in a tiny, two-person airplane.
You can also view the falls by foot, car, or train via the Victoria Falls Bridge, a single-span steel arch bridge connecting Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Built in 1905, the bridge is still one of only a few spanning these two countries' borders.
From the Victoria Falls Bridge, I bet you could get an excellent view of one of those big rainbows Mr. Fay showed us.
Oh darn! The rainbow outside is gone already. But that's how most things are in nature, right? They're always changing.
The Zambezi River doesn't look the same two years in a row, and Victoria Falls doesn't look the same in February as it does in November.
But I hope the falls don't change too much because I want to hop into Devil's Pool one day! See you next week!

. It's about some magical dragons that protect the kingdom of the Golden
Emperor. Oh, that reminds me! I want to tell you about our latest landmarks
lesson. Yesterday in Mr. Fay's class, we learned about an awesome place in Beijing,

world. And get this: the complex is decorated with thousands of cool-looking dragons, too many of them to even
count! Construction of the Forbidden City began in 1406, when the third emperor from the Ming dynasty decided to build a new palace complex in the city of

City. But what's really amazing is how the workers moved some of the building
materials. To transport heavy blocks of stone thousands of miles, workers created ice paths by pouring water on the frozen
ground. The slippery ice made it much easier to drag the stone blocks
along. And then, when huge logs needed to be moved for some of the buildings, guess what the workers did . .

Wow! Chinese emperors continued living in the Forbidden City until 1912, when the Chinese Revolution ended imperial
rule. The last emperor, Puyi, was only about six years old at the
time. And for the next 12 years, he and his family were basically imprisoned inside the Forbidden
City. By now you’re probably wondering why the palace complex is called the Forbidden
City. Well, Mr. Fay explained that it was because most people were forbidden from entering
it. Even members of the imperial family were restricted from some
areas. There was only one person who could go wherever he wanted in the complex—the emperor
himself! Still today the first thing you notice as you approach the Forbidden City are the enormous red walls—almost ten meters high—surrounding the

entrance. This gate has five different doors, but back in imperial times, people couldn’t just walk through any door they

door. Inside the Forbidden City there are two main areas: the Outer Court and the Inner Court.

No wonder the Forbidden City is so huge!
Just beyond the Inner Court is the Imperial Garden with fishponds, sculptures, and a small temple.
Mr. Fay said the garden was a place where emperors could relax and meditate.
I wonder if they spent a lot of time out there—if you ask me, ruling a whole empire sounds pretty stressful!
While the buildings in the Forbidden City are all scarlet in color, the roofs are lined with yellow tiles since yellow symbolized the emperor’s power.
Many of the decorations inside the palaces are yellow or gold too, including the bricks used for the floors.
Remember what I said earlier about all the dragons inside the Forbidden City?
Well, we found out that dragons symbolize important imperial characteristics such as benevolence, excellence, and heroism.
That's why the Forbidden City has so many of them.
There's an incredible "dragon pavement" with dragons carved out of stone; dragon statues perched on top of rooftops; and the Nine Dragon Screen, a really famous glazed tile screen.
If you ever get to see the screen, you might notice that one tile looks slightly different from the rest.
That's because right before an emperor was going to inspect the screen, a tile broke.
So the craftsmen, who didn’t want to get in trouble, quickly made a wooden tile and stuck it in place. Luckily the emperor never noticed!
Each year millions of tourists visit the Forbidden City.
Many head to the Palace Museum to see artifacts from imperial China such as precious silks, jewelry, porcelain, jade, bronzes, and other valuable works of art.
Today a lot of the buildings inside the Forbidden City are set up just as they were hundreds of years ago.
According to Mr. Fay, that makes it easy to imagine the royal court back in the days when servants, couriers, and important government officials were bustling around.

And speaking of forts, this week in our landmarks lesson, we learned about a really famous one: the Kremlin in Moscow, Russia.
Lots of Russian cities have a kremlin —the Russian word for fortress or fort—but the one in Moscow is so famous that most people just call it the
Kremlin. The Kremlin is an enormous collection of buildings that's shaped kind of like a
triangle. And with its amazing cathedrals, palaces, and tall, colorful towers, the Kremlin is often described as an "architectural
wonder." When it was first built back in 1156, the Kremlin was just a small wooden
fortress. Over time more buildings were added to the site, especially during the fifteenth
century. That was when a czar named Ivan the Great ruled Russia, and he wanted to show off his power by expanding the
place. Later other Russian rulers rebuilt some of the structures and added even more buildings to the
grounds. Since this expansion occurred over a few centuries, there's now a huge variety of architectural styles at the
Kremlin. The entire complex is surrounded by thick brick walls that have twenty towers built into
them. Each tower is unique with its own
name. The oldest of these is the Secret Tower, named this because it used to contain a secret tunnel that led to the Moskva
River. So even if the Kremlin had been completely surrounded by an enemy army, people could have still sneaked to the river to get
water! At the very center of the Kremlin is Cathedral Square, a large open space surrounded by—you guessed
it—cathedrals! In fact, many people think these buildings are among the most beautiful churches in the
world. The Cathedral of the Assumption is the oldest and largest of
these. Unfortunately, when the cathedral was almost complete, it was destroyed by an
earthquake. However, work on the cathedral was continued, and in 1479 it was finally
finished. The Cathedral of the Assumption is a massive building topped with five golden onion
domes. The domes are called this because they look like . . . well, onions, of
course! According to Mr. Fay, onion domes are very common in Russian
architecture. Another cathedral at the square, the Cathedral of the Annunciation, was used as a private chapel for the
czars. Except there was one czar who wasn't allowed to enter it—Ivan the
Terrible. Back then, according to the Russian Orthodox Church, a person could be married only three

church. Guess what Ivan the Terrible did to solve the problem . . . He added a porch to the building!

The Czar Bell, the largest bell in the world, sits at the foot of this tower.

Today about two-thirds of the Kremlin is used for official government business.

It holds lots of priceless artifacts collected by Russian czars over the centuries—swords, armor, pistols, clothing, jewelry, carriages, even Ivan the Terrible's throne!
Visitors to the Armory can also check out the State Diamond Fund, a collection of Russian gems that includes the largest sapphire in the world.
The State Kremlin Palace is another building that's open to the public.
Built in the 1960s, this building is the newest one inside the complex.
In fact, Mr. Fay said that its plain, straight lines and tall, modern windows make it look out of place among the older buildings.
It has a huge 6,000-seat auditorium, which is used today as a concert hall.
If you ever go to the Kremlin, you'll also see another important world landmark: Red Square.
This large public space sits just outside the Kremlin's entrance and it was once the site of battles and military parades.
But now it's used mainly for things like rock concerts and fashion shows.
I bet it's a cool place to see a concert!
At one end of the square is St. Basil's Cathedral, which Ivan the Terrible commissioned to celebrate a military victory.
This cathedral is known for its brightly colored onion domes.
Each dome has a unique color pattern and texture, giving the cathedral an extremely distinct appearance.
Supposedly Ivan the Terrible wanted to make sure that the architect who designed the cathedral never built anything more beautiful than St. Basil's.
So when the cathedral was finished, Ivan had him blinded!

Hi, Little Fox readers! It's me, Jake! This weekend my family and I are going to New York City to visit my cousin.
He goes to college there, and guess what—I just found out that Mr. Fay went to the same college!
Our teacher loved living in New York, and he said he especially loved going to Central Park.
Then Mr. Fay's face lit up, and he said that Central Park would make a great subject for a landmarks lesson!
Located in the middle of Manhattan, Central Park is one of the most famous parks in the world.
This 3.4-square kilometer park contains rocky hills, lakes, ponds, open meadows, dense woodlands—things you'd never expect to find in a bustling city with millions of residents!
And amazingly, almost all of the landscape was created artificially.
The idea for a large public park in New York started in the 1840s.
The city's population was growing fast, and a lot of rich people wanted a quiet place where they could escape from the crowds and the noise, and just enjoy nature.
Park planners selected a large area of swampland and rocky bluffs in the middle of the city.
About 1,600 poor immigrants and freed slaves lived there in shantytowns, mostly farming and raising livestock, until about 1853.
That was when the city's government was authorized to take over the land, and they began forcing everyone off it.
Park commissioners held a landscape design contest and received 33 submissions.
In 1858 judges chose a plan by a landscape designer, Frederick Law Olmsted, and Calvert Vaux, an architect.
Inspired by parks in England, the plan harmoniously blended man-made elements with natural elements.
Over twenty thousand workers spent about three years creating the park's landscape.
They used 150 metric tons of gunpowder to blast away giant boulders.
They also filled in swampy areas, created seven bodies of water, and planted nearly three hundred thousand trees.
When the park was finished, it contained a wide, tree-lined avenue and an enormous terrace and fountain.
Separate paths for walking, horseback riding, and carriage driving were laid out around the park.
Thirty-six unique bridges allowed these paths to cross over and under each other, so that everyone could enjoy the natural surroundings without bumping into each other.
At first Central Park was used mainly by rich people, who rode their carriages along the park's roads.
Most of the city's poorer residents lived too far from the park to visit easily.
Plus, park commissioners created lots of rules that made it difficult for working class people to use the space.
People weren't allowed to play any sports on the lawns, and group picnics weren't permitted.
Drivers of commercial wagons couldn’t take them into the park, and events such as concerts were never held on Sundays, the one day of the week when working class people didn't have to work.
Over time these rules were eliminated, as more and more people protested them. By
the end of the nineteenth century, people of all social classes were visiting the park to picnic, play ball games, and attend Sunday concerts. Today
Central Park is much more than just a place to enjoy nature. It
contains a large number of sculptures, memorials, and fountains scattered throughout the area. Each
year thirty-eight million people visit for activities like running, biking, swimming, bird watching, rock climbing, concerts—even roller-skating dance parties! The
park has 21 playgrounds, a zoo, a carousel, an ice-skating rink, boat rentals, restaurants, a puppet theater, and wide lawns where visitors can play Frisbee or just lie in the sun. An
enormous reservoir, which holds over 3.5 million cubic meters of water, takes up about an eighth of the parkland. Even
though it no longer supplies New York City with drinking water, this reservoir is still an important part of the city. Mr.
Fay said it's a wonderful place to watch the sun set, and if you're feeling energetic, you can go running on the 2.5-kilometer track that loops around it. The
track is a famous spot in New York City; it's even been featured in books, TV shows, and movies. In
the summer the park's open-air Delacorte Theater is home to Shakespeare in the Park, a program that features performances of Shakespeare's works as well as other plays and musicals. Tickets
are free, but if you want one, you'd better get there early—Shakespeare in the Park is very popular! Also
located in the park is the Metropolitan Museum of Art, one of the world's most well-known art museums. I
love to draw, so I was really excited to find that out! Mr. Fay told us that Central Park's oldest structure is right behind the museum. It's
a tall Egyptian obelisk called Cleopatra's Needle, and it was built in—get this—1450 BC !
Egypt gave it to the U.S. as a gift in 1877, and four years later, the obelisk was carefully erected in Central Park.
Most kids' favorite spot in the park is the Central Park Zoo.
It's open all year and is home to over 130 different species, including polar bears, snow monkeys, penguins, and leafcutter ants.
The zoo has a special children's section where little kids can feed goats and other farm animals.
A very popular attraction at the zoo is feeding time at the sea lion pool!

Despite all these fun things to do and see in Central Park, Mr. Fay said he likes nothing better than buying a soft pretzel from a street vendor, sitting on a park bench, and just watching people go by.
Well, I should start packing for my trip.
I'm sure there's a lot my family and I can do in New York City, but there's just one place I want to go—Central Park!
See you next week!
Hello, again! It's Alex here. I'm at the library right now researching one of the world landmarks we learned about this year in Mr. Fay's class.
Mr. Fay gave everyone in the class an object that represents a landmark.
I got this one: a mini ship filled with cargo containers. Can you guess which world landmark it represents?
That's right! This mini ship represents the Panama Canal, an international waterway that is also one of the seven modern wonders of the world.
The canal is located in central Panama, which is the southernmost country in Central America.
The country itself is on an isthmus—a strip of land connecting two larger pieces of land.
Mr. Fay told us that Panama connects North and South America.
But here is what the country is most famous for: its east coast borders the Atlantic Ocean, and its west coast borders the Pacific Ocean.
You're probably wondering why Panama's location is such a big deal.
Well, here's why it eventually became really important to sailors and traders around the world.
Remember the European explorers who arrived in the Americas in the 1500s?
Mr. Fay said that their explorations led to settlements and the start of many new international trade routes.
But sailors who wanted to cross from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean had to travel along the southern end of South America to get around the continent.
This journey took months, and sailors had to navigate around fierce winds, floating icebergs, and rocky shores.
Many sailors did not survive the trip.
For hundreds of years, people had been looking for an easier way to travel from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
People tried creating land routes through Panama, including a railroad.
Finally, in 1880, the French decided to dig a canal.
Led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, the builder of the Suez Canal, the French planned to dig a sea-level canal.
But digging that canal proved to be nearly impossible.
Panama has a long rainy season, and the land was covered with dense, tropical jungles.
Then there was the mighty Chagres River, which wound its way through Panama with a wild flow that grew even more unpredictable when it rained.
Mr. Fay showed us a slide show of the dirty, tired workers who dug and blasted the earth all day long.
Mosquitoes were everywhere, spreading devastating diseases like malaria and yellow fever.
Mudslides from the rain were a constant problem.
Finally, after twenty thousand workers had died, and investors had lost lots of money, the French decided to stop digging.
But American President Theodore Roosevelt wasn't ready to give up on the project yet.
He saw the canal as vitally important to his country, a way for America to gain prosperity through international trading.
In 1904 the American effort began. Of course, the Americans faced all the problems that had defeated the French.
But the Americans quickly realized something important: there was no way to complete the project without creating healthy conditions for the workers.
So they made this a priority, sanitizing workers' living spaces and spraying pesticides to kill the disease-carrying mosquitoes.
Over five thousand workers died, but the death toll could have been much higher.
The Americans also made a huge change in the canal's engineering.
Instead of digging one that was sea level, they decided to construct a "lake-and-lock" canal.
Most of the kids in our class—including me—had no idea what a "lake-and-lock" canal is.
Mr. Fay explained that a lock is part of a canal with a gate at each end.
The gates can be opened and closed to control the canal's water level.
The Americans' idea was to dam the Chagres River to create a huge lake.
Then a series of locks could be used to raise ships from the Atlantic Ocean to the lake's level.
The ships could cross the lake, and drop down again through another set of locks to reach the Pacific Ocean.
If you ask me, using locks in the Panama Canal was an ingenious idea.
But Americans weren't the only ones who had thought of it.
A French engineer had proposed the same thing about thirty years earlier, at the same meeting where de Lesseps proposed his sea-level canal.
In 1914, when the Panama Canal opened at last, the locks system worked flawlessly!
About 82 kilometers long, the waterway finally provided safe passage for ships from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
In the canal's first year, one thousand ships traveled through it—international shipping and trade would never be the same again!
Today about 14,000 ships and over 300 million tons of cargo pass through the canal each year.
I had to research what is in those long, colorful shipping containers, and here's what I learned: oil, grains, metals, and coal make up a lot of the cargo.
Bananas and automobiles are often in the containers too.
It's not just cargo ships traveling along the canal; you can take the 15-40 hour trip aboard a luxury cruise ship.
The amazing brains of the engineers who dreamed up the canal, along with the heroic work of over eighty thousand laborers, helped to make the Panama Canal one of the modern wonders of the world.
Mr. Fay called it "a triumph of man over nature."
And there are plans to change the canal again.
A seven-year expansion plan that includes adding more locks was launched in 2007.
It will allow even more ships to pass through the canal.
Whew! I feel like someone opened the locks on me and flooded my brain with too much information!
The library will be closing soon, so I should get going.
But one last thing: President Roosevelt never even got to see the finished canal. Isn't that sad?
I guess being the president of the U.S. is a big job, and he was really busy.
See you soon, Little Fox readers!
Hi, Little Fox readers! It's me, Mellissa, again.
My little brother just asked me to take a picture of his plastic army soldiers. He has them lined up outside in straight long rows.
They look kind of like the cool landmark Mr. Fay told us about this week: the Terra-cotta Army in China's Shaanxi province.
The Terra-cotta soldiers are a lot bigger than my brother's plastic toys, though. They're life-size and made of clay.
In fact, this ancient massive army is considered one of the world's greatest archaeological discoveries and was even declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.
The Terra-cotta Army was created during the reign of Emperor Qin Shihuangdi.
In 221 B.C., Qin Shihuangdi—who was just a king at the time—managed to conquer and unify China's warring states and proclaim himself China's first emperor.
He was a brutal leader who had lots of people executed and trusted almost no one.
But he also accomplished some pretty impressive things.
He standardized the area's weights and measures, laws, written language, weapons—even the length of axles on carts!
Under his orders new fortresses were constructed, along with a series of defensive walls that eventually became the Great Wall of China.
In addition, he instructed workers to build an underground funerary compound for himself.
That's where he would be buried after death.
Mr. Fay told us that Qin Shihuangdi's tomb was huge—about fifty square kilometers!
According to a famous historian, it contained a small-scale model of the world with miniature palaces, trees carved from jade, even flowing rivers and an ocean. Mercury
was used for the water, and pearls were attached to the ceiling to represent stars. In
order to protect the tomb from robbers, workers rigged crossbows that would automatically fire if anyone entered. Before
Qin Shihuangdi's reign, it was customary for a ruler's entire royal court to be slaughtered and buried with him, so that they could continue to serve him in the afterlife. However,
this practice had long been abandoned by the emperor's time, so he decided to use clay statues instead. Qin
Shihuangdi also ordered his workers to build a clay army that could guard his tomb after he died—this became the Terra-cotta army. The
army includes a huge assortment of soldiers—at least eight thousand infantry, cavalry, archers, officers—all in battle formation and organized according to military rank. The
statues' bodies are pretty similar, but each warrior has unique details such as hats, mustaches, shoes, and hair. While
some of the warriors look fierce and ready for battle, others appear pretty calm. They
were originally armed with real bronze weapons like swords, spears, and axes. Some
are even crouching, ready to fire the working crossbows they once held. In
addition to the warriors, there are also life-size horses and chariots. Some
scholars have assumed that the statues are portraits of actual soldiers. It's
more likely, however, that they don't represent specific people, but rather, all the various ethnic groups in China. Approximately
one thousand craftsmen worked for 11 years to make the statues from terra-cotta, a type of clay. All
the soldiers' legs were cast in similar molds, but for the upper bodies and arms, different types of molds were used, to vary the soldiers' head and body shapes. After
the body sections were pulled out of the molds, expert sculptors refined them, adding all sorts of minute details to make the statues look unique and lifelike. And
get this: every warrior has the name of the sculptor who made it. At
first I assumed the artists were proud of their work and wanted to sign it. But
Mr. Fay said they really did it so their work could be checked for quality. The
emperor insisted that any statue that wasn't perfect had to be redone, or worse, he would have the sculptor— gulp —executed! Talk about
pressure! After all the carving was finished, the statues were dried in a kiln, and then coated in a thick layer of
lacquer. Next workers painted them in rich, bright
colors. The finished statues were carried down ramps to narrow underground halls, where they were put into
position. Then the halls were sealed off and hidden from
view. For over two thousand years, nobody saw the Terra-cotta
Army. In fact, it wasn't mentioned in historical texts, so nobody even knew it existed.
Then in 1974 some peasants stumbled across fragments of a clay statue in the ground while digging a well.
Government archaeologists began excavating the site, and discovered an enormous underground pit, containing thousands of the clay soldiers.
Eventually more pits were found, each containing many soldiers and horses.
Excavation has continued at the site ever since the discovery of the Terra-cotta Army.
The first three pits that were found have been enclosed in large buildings and are now the Museum of the Terracotta Army.
What's really cool about this museum is that it's still a functioning archaeological site.
So visitors to the museum can actually see the excavation process.
Unfortunately it hasn't been easy to safely dig up the Terra-cotta Army.
When a statue is exposed to the air, the lacquer on its surface immediately shrinks and peels away from the clay, taking the pigment with it.
Archaeologists unearthing these statues sometimes have just minutes to try to preserve the color before it's gone forever.
Because of this and other difficulties, the excavation has been a very slow process;
as of 2012 archaeologists hadn't done any excavation of the tomb itself—they're afraid they might damage it.
Well, I have to get going now. My brother wants me to take that picture of his army before he knocks it down with his remote control army tank!
See you next week!
Hey, Little Fox readers. It's me, Alex, again. I just got back from ice hockey practice; our coach showed us how to use the neutral zone trap.
That's a strategy to keep the other team trapped in the middle of the hockey rink.
The trap is supposed to stop opposing players from entering our zone and scoring goals.
But I wanted to tell you about another zone we just learned about from Mr. Fay.
It's the Demilitarized Zone, or DMZ, which separates North and South Korea.
Even though it's referred to as a de militarized zone, the DMZ is the most heavily fortified border in the
world. You probably already know this, but Korea wasn't always divided into two separate countries. During World War II, Japan controlled
Korea. When Japan lost the war, the Soviet Union and United States temporarily took control of the peninsula, with the Soviet Union in the North and the United Sates in the
South. By 1948 two separate countries had been formed—the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) and the Republic of Korea (South
Korea). The two nations were divided along the earth's 38th parallel, or 38 degrees north of the
equator. Each side claimed to be the legitimate government of all of
Korea. Then in 1950 North Korea invaded South Korea, with help from the Soviet
Union. The South fought back, aided by the United States, as well as the United
Nations. Fighting continued for three years, until the two sides finally reached a cease-fire
agreement. The 1953 cease-fire agreement reestablished the border between the two countries near the 38th
parallel. This border became known as the Military Demarcation Line, or
MDL. Both sides pulled back two kilometers from the MDL, leaving a four-kilometer buffer zone—the DMZ—between the two
nations. Today this buffer zone is an extremely dangerous place, with razor wire, watchtowers, heavy artillery, and soldiers lined up along both its northern and southern
boundaries. Soldiers are allowed to patrol inside the DMZ, but they are not allowed to cross the
MDL. The only place in the DMZ where soldiers from the two Koreas face each other is the Joint Security Area
(JSA). Built on the village of Panmunjom, the JSA is bisected by the MDL, which is marked with a low concrete
slab. The JSA contains a small number of buildings, including watchtowers and several low blue buildings owned by the
U.N. Diplomatic talks between North and South Korea are sometimes held in a conference room inside one of these U.N.
buildings. In order to be stationed in the JSA, a South Korean soldier must hold a black belt in either taekwondo or judo and be at least 177 cm
tall. The South Korean soldiers guard the area with fists clenched and stony facial
expressions. They also wear mirrored sunglasses, which prevents them from staring directly into the eyes of North Korean
troops. Mr. Fay said that could lead to a dangerous conflict!
North Korea also puts only highly trained soldiers in the JSA.
Like the South Korean soldiers, the North Korean troops assume a rigid military stance.
Despite the cease-fire agreement, a few violent incidents have occurred in the DMZ over the years.
One especially tragic event happened in 1976, when a small group of South Korean and American soldiers were pruning a tree to improve their view of a checkpoint.
After ordering the troops to stop, North Korean soldiers attacked and murdered two American officers with axes.
To avoid reigniting the war, South Korea and the U.S. decided not to retaliate with military force.
Instead a large group of soldiers returned to the site three days later and cut the tree down completely.
Mr. Fay told us that secret tunnels have also been discovered under the DMZ.
In 1974 a South Korean patrol group discovered the first one, which had electricity, lighting, sleeping areas, and storage areas for weapons.
Since then even more tunnels have been found.
Today the landscape in the DMZ consists of wetlands, forests, mountains, and big open fields.
If it hadn't become the DMZ back in 1953, the land probably would have been developed by now.
But instead the area has become an amazing wildlife sanctuary.
In the DMZ you can see flying squirrels, along with very rare animals like Asiatic black bears and Chinese gorals.
Two of the most endangered bird species in the world—the white-naped crane and the red-crowned crane—have also been spotted here.
By now most of the land in South Korea has been developed, and North Korea's landscape has suffered from severe deforestation.
So environmental groups want to preserve this pristine ecosystem, even if Korea becomes unified again.
The DMZ may be the front line between two countries that are technically still at war, but it has also become a popular tourist destination.
About 100,000 people visit the JSA each year, with tour guides taking many of them into the U.N. conference room and even into the secret tunnels.
If you ever travel to the DMZ, you'll need to remember that soldiers across the MDL are watching you.
You can only look in certain directions, and you need permission before taking pictures.
Under no circumstances can you point or wave at anyone on the other side of the border.
Both sides are ready to fight at a moment's notice, so you have to avoid doing anything that could be misinterpreted!
The DMZ definitely sounds dangerous, but I'd really like to visit it one day.
Mr. Fay described it as one of the most unique and fascinating places in the world—a place where two countries are divided by a line that cannot be crossed.
Well, Little Fox readers, I'd better get ready for bed now. My hockey team has a big game tomorrow.
Hey . . . maybe we'll get a chance to use the neutral zone trap—and win the game!
Hi, everyone! It's me, Melissa, again. Today in science class, we started a fun engineering project.
We built towers, using just Jell-O, straws, and cardboard.
Tomorrow we're going to shake our towers to see which ones can withstand the force of earthquakes.
Designing a strong tower was definitely pretty tricky.
It reminded me of a landmark we learned about in Mr. Fay's class this week: the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco, California.
The Golden Gate is one of the most famous bridges in the world.
But before its construction began, lots of people thought it would be impossible to build. I'll explain why in a minute.
First I have to tell you a little bit about the city's geography.
San Francisco sits on a small peninsula between the Pacific Ocean and the San Francisco Bay, which are connected by the Golden Gate strait.
By the early twentieth century, the city had become very crowded, and city officials wanted to make the trip across the strait easier for city residents.
For years a ferry service had taken people back and forth.
But by the early twentieth century, the ferries were very crowded, with long lines.
Of course, the obvious solution was to build a suspension bridge across the water.
That's a bridge with a roadway held up by towers and heavy-duty cables.
In San Francisco there was just one problem: the Golden Gate strait is a terrible place to build a bridge!
Strong winds blow through the strait, and waters flowing down from the mountains collide with the incoming tide, creating turbulent currents and dense fog.
Plus, the Golden Gate Strait sits close to a major fault line where earthquakes can occur. It sounds pretty dangerous, right?
Still, by 1916 city officials were determined to forge ahead.
A bridge builder named Joseph Strauss was hired, and he began working with a team of engineers and designers.
His vision was to create a bridge that could handle the harsh conditions in the strait and yet also serve as an image of beauty.
Construction began in 1933, right in the middle of the Great Depression, when many people were unemployed and desperate to find work.
Ironworkers from all over the country arrived in San Francisco, hoping to get a job working on the bridge.
Even people just pretending to be ironworkers arrived!
Workers had to deal with the strait's nasty weather, slippery surfaces, and dizzying heights.
On top of all that, they were using dangerous materials like extremely hot rivets and air hammers, which required special skill to operate.
From the start, Strauss was very concerned about his workers' safety.
The Golden Gate Bridge was the first major construction project where workers wore hard hats, a new invention at the time.
Strauss also insisted that everyone hook themselves to safety ropes, firing anyone who refused to do so.
And he had a huge net placed under the bridge. During
the four years of construction, 19 workers fell into the net—that's 19 lives that were saved! However,
construction of the Golden Gate Bridge didn't go entirely smoothly. A
trestle being used to access one of the towers was destroyed twice, first by a ship lost in the fog, and then by strong winds. And
despite all the safety precautions, 11 workers died. For the first three years, only one man was killed. Then
in February 1937, a large piece of scaffolding fell, killing ten more men. Bridges
are usually painted gray or silver, but the Golden Gate Bridge needed a color that would stand out in the thick San Francisco fog. Mr.
Fay said the U.S. Navy wanted to paint the bridge with black and yellow stripes. Even
though that might have looked cool, I think international orange, which was developed just for the bridge, is perfect. It's
visible in the fog, and it looks beautiful against the blue water and surrounding green and brown hills. By
May of 1937, the bridge was complete. Workers
had used more than 75,000,000 kilograms of steel, 129,000 kilometers of cable, and nearly 298,000 cubic meters of concrete. At
the time the Golden Gate Bridge was the longest and tallest suspension bridge in the world. On
opening day pedestrians, runners, people on unicycles, and even on stilts, showed up to celebrate and travel across the bridge. I
was surprised to learn that the bridge is still being worked on all the time. The
fog and salty ocean air constantly eat away the bridge's steel. So

My aunt just got back from a trip to Italy, and she brought me this feather mask from Venice. It's pretty cool, huh?
Did you know that the city of Venice is famous for its fancy masks?
But that's not all it's famous for.
Venice is often called the "Floating City" because it was built on a group of 118 small islands.
It looks like the city floats magically on top of the water!
We learned all about Venice this year during one of Mr. Fay's landmarks lessons.
Located in a lagoon in the Adriatic Sea, Venice used to be a powerful maritime republic.
Many people think it's still the most beautiful—and amazing—city in the world.
Historians believe that Venice's earliest residents were fishermen and salt workers.
Then, during the fifth century, others began fleeing to the islands to escape raids by barbarians.
Over time the islands in the lagoon united to form a republic, and by 727, the first doge, or duke, had been selected to govern it.
From the ninth through the fifteenth centuries, the Republic of Venice flourished, serving as Europe's main center of trade—the place where silk, spices, and other valuable goods arrived from Asia.
Many wealthy Venetians were patrons of the arts.
That encouraged glassmakers, painters, musicians, and of course, mask-makers to create many beautiful works during this time.
By the end of the fifteenth century, however, the Republic of Venice began to decline.
Ottoman Turks had been seizing lots of nearby land.
Plus, other European countries started to discover new trade routes, breaking up Venice's empire along the coast.
The Republic finally collapsed in 1797 when Napoleon's army conquered it.
Then, in 1886, Venice became part of the Kingdom of Italy.
If you ask me, the most interesting thing about Venice—besides its fancy masks—is the city's unusual geography.
The archipelago sits in a shallow lagoon with more than two hundred canals linking together to form a huge waterway system.
A row of sandbanks shelters the lagoon from the open sea. Openings in these sandbanks allow traffic (and tides) to flow in and out of the city.
If you've ever been to Venice, you probably know that there are only two ways to get around—by boat or by foot.
Because of its narrow streets and canals, no cars are permitted in the city.
Mr. Fay told us that traveling by boat is lots of fun.
The Grand Canal, which is Venice's longest waterway, cuts through the heart of the city.
It's constantly busy, filled with all kinds of noisy traffic—motor-powered water buses and taxis, mail boats, fruit barges, even fire, police, ambulance, and garbage boats!
The most famous type of boat in Venice is definitely the gondola, the black, flat-bottomed boat that's considered a symbol of the city.
Propelled by gondoliers, or drivers who use long poles to steer, gondolas are really popular with tourists.
But we learned something sad about these ancient boats—there are only a few hundred left.
Gondolas are very expensive to build, and today very few people know how to carve them.
For pedestrians, Venice has nearly four hundred canal bridges, which means you can get nearly anywhere in Venice by walking!
Many of the bridges are marble, sculpted hundreds of years ago.
Lots of people enjoy sightseeing from the Rialto Bridge with its great view of the traffic in the Grand Canal.
Another famous bridge is called the Bridge of Sighs.
The poet, Lord Byron, named it that because convicts used to cross it on their way to imprisonment.
As Bryon imagined it, the convicts would sigh with sadness as they took one last look at lovely Venice—and their freedom!
Other popular tourist sites include the Doge's Palace, which was the doges' home and the political center of life in Venice, and St. Mark's Basilica.
St. Mark's is an old church that once served as the doges' private chapel.
In front of the basilica is St. Mark's Plaza, a square lined with historic buildings, cafes, and shops.
The square is nearly always packed with tourists, as well as hungry pigeons!
I asked my aunt why masks are such a popular souvenir from Venice.
She explained that masks have probably been part of Venice's history since the thirteenth century.
Historians believe Venetians sometimes wore them to disguise their social class and gender.
Masks were also worn during Carnival, the Christian festival that takes place before the holy season of Lent.
In fact, people today still celebrate Carnival in Venice by wearing elaborate masks.
Mr. Fay said you can see some really . . . um . . . unusual ones there!
Today tourism is Venice's main industry.
All those tourists help to keep Venice's economy healthy, but they've also brought problems to the city, like huge crowds and very high prices.
Another serious problem for the "Floating City" is that it's sinking!
The city has had several devastating floods, and with the sea level rising in the Adriatic Sea, officials worry that flooding will grow even worse.
So city planners have halted development and relocated historic buildings to higher ground.
And engineers have been working for decades to construct an elaborate barrier system with huge metal gates to hold back the tides.
I think lots of people want to make sure that Venice—with all its unique beauty—is preserved for future generations.
According to Mr. Fay, it's not only one of the oldest tourist sites in the world, but it has also captured the imagination of poets, painters, and filmmakers for centuries.
The poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow once called it a "white phantom city, whose untrodden streets are rivers and whose pavements are the shifting shadows of palaces."
That's a pretty awesome description, don't you think?

Hi, Little Fox readers! It's Alex here. I just got back from a whole day of rock climbing with my dad. Boy, it was fun!
When we got to the top of the tallest rock, there was a fantastic view of our town. We also spotted a hawk's nest!
The climbing that Dad and I did today was pretty easy, but someday I want to climb some serious rock formations, like El Capitan or Half Dome.
They're huge granite monoliths in Yosemite National Park, a landmark we learned about this week in Mr. Fay's class.
The park is located in the Sierra Nevada, a mountain range in California. It's one of the oldest wilderness parks in the United States.
Mr. Fay has been to Yosemite, and he showed our class some of his photos.
We saw towering cliffs and waterfalls, deep valleys, fast-moving rivers, lakes, wild animals, mountain meadows, and giant trees.
Of course, Yosemite wasn't always a national park. For thousands of years, Yosemite Valley was home to several groups of Native Americans.
But in 1851 a group of white soldiers arrived to force them from the land.
As word of Yosemite's incredible beauty spread, more people visited the valley.
One of them was James Mason Hutchings, who believed he could make a lot of money running a hotel for adventurous tourists.
Hutchings invited a photographer to the valley in 1859.
Once the American public saw pictures of Yosemite's amazing landscape, the valley became a popular tourist destination.
Mr. Fay told us the person who's most closely associated with Yosemite is John Muir, a naturalist.
Muir arrived in Yosemite in 1868 and fell in love with the place, living there on and off for the next six years.
Muir also grew concerned about the damage that grazing livestock had caused to Yosemite's grassy highlands and how quickly its forests were being chopped down.
But by then Yosemite had an even bigger problem: tourists, and lots of them.
Garbage was piling up in the valley, and people had carved tunnels through the trunks of some of the enormous trees.
Muir wrote about the problems he saw, and he also urged the U.S. government to protect Yosemite.
Thanks to Muir's determination, Yosemite National Park was established in 1890.
Today over three million people visit Yosemite National Park each year. The most popular section of the park is Yosemite Valley.
Many of Yosemite's famous waterfalls are here, including Yosemite Falls, the tallest waterfall in North America.
If you go and see this waterfall during a full moon in spring, you might get to see a moonbow.
That's just like a rainbow, except the colors are created by the light from the moon!
Millions of years ago, massive glaciers sculpted this 13-kilometer valley, carving the granite into Yosemite's unique smooth domes and sheer walls.
Rock climbers from all over the world come to Yosemite Valley to scale these walls.
Mr. Fay showed us some photos of people climbing El Capitan—they were really high up! There was even a tent hanging halfway up the rock.
Apparently most climbers need more than a day to climb the whole thing, so they set up bivouacs, or temporary campsites, right on the side of the wall!
A lot of the big walls in Yosemite are only for advanced climbers. But beginners can have fun there too.
A school offers rock-climbing classes for people of all different levels.
When I asked Mr. Fay if he took a class, he said, "No way—I prefer to keep my feet on the ground!"
To get to the top of Yosemite's monoliths, you don't have to be a rock climber; many of the mountains have hiking trails too.
But that doesn't mean it's easy to reach the top! The trail up Half Dome is extremely difficult.
In fact, the last 120 meters are so steep and slippery, you have to pull yourself up along some steel cables.
Hundreds of people hike up Half Dome each day, and the trail gets crowded. So if you're brave enough to try it, start early!
Another major attraction in Yosemite is Mariposa Grove.
At heights exceeding fifty meters, the giant sequoias in this grove are some of the tallest trees in the world.
I'll bet that walking along the trail through the grove makes people feel pretty tiny.
One tree, the Grizzly Giant, is believed to be over two thousand years old.
Another tree, known as the "Telescope tree," suffered severe fires and eventually became hollow.
Amazingly, the tree is still alive—you can go inside it and see right up to the sky.
The grove has a few trees that have fallen down too.
Some of them fell more than two hundred years ago, but they're still intact because sequoias are extremely resistant to decay.
Mr. Fay told us Yosemite is really crowded. Cars often clog the roads and tourists are everywhere.
So during his visit, he hopped on to one of the park's free shuttle buses and went to Tuolumne Meadows.
This area of the park receives fewer visitors than the valley, which makes it the perfect place to be alone and enjoy nature.
You can sit and listen to the Tuolumne River, look at the mountains in the distance, wander through a field of wildflowers, or watch the sky for birds like Prairie falcons and Great gray owls.
For people who don't want to climb the huge monoliths in the valley, Tuolumne Meadows has some smaller rock formations.
They're much easier to climb but still provide some pretty impressive views.
Well, it's time for me to get cleaned up and put away my climbing gear.
Then I'm going to send Jake some of the photos I took today. Wait till he sees my photo of a cool snake!
Hello, Little Fox readers. It’s Jake, and I have a new landmark to share with you.
Mr. Fay taught us about Tokyo Tower yesterday, and he even created a virtual tour for us to take online!
The virtual tour is pretty awesome. I found out that Tokyo Tower is the world’s largest self-supporting steel tower.
It's located right in the heart of Tokyo, Japan, the largest metropolitan area in the world.
Modeled after the Eiffel Tower in Paris, France, Tokyo Tower stands at 333 meters—that's 13 meters higher than the Eiffel Tower.
And it has a pretty interesting history.
Back in the late 1950s, Japan’s national broadcasting system was expanding, and an antenna was needed to transmit television signals.
Architects designed Tokyo Tower to take care of that need, but the tower soon served a bigger purpose too.
During World War II, Tokyo had been firebombed, destroying much of the city.
With its bright orange-and-white stripes of paint, the tall tower rose up from the ruins like a shining beam of hope.
It became a monument of Japanese pride, giving the citizens of Tokyo faith that Japan was strong enough to rebuild itself after the war.
Mr. Fay told us that the tower was painted in bright colors so that airplane pilots could easily spot it during the day.
The entire tower must be repainted every five years, using 28,000 liters of paint.
At night the tower’s 176 floodlights illuminate its steel beams, shining orange in winter and white in summer.
This makes it an impressive sight in the city’s skyline.
I asked Mr. Fay why it’s called a "self-supporting" structure, and he explained that a lot of tall antenna towers need to be stabilized with steel wires anchored to the ground.
But Tokyo Tower is incredibly sturdy and can stand on its own.
Engineers designed it to be able to withstand Japan’s many earthquakes, along with winds of up to one hundred meters per second.
Since the tower is now over fifty years old, those engineers must have done a very good job!
Mr. Fay's virtual tour started at FootTown, which is a four-story building directly under the tower.
As I toured the first floor, I could see the first of many souvenir shops selling local cakes and pastries.
There's also an aquarium, featuring over fifty thousand kinds of fish, from all over the world.
A food court occupies the second floor of FootTown, where you can eat anything from Japanese noodles to McDonald’s hamburgers.
The third floor has a wax museum, with sculptures imported from London—including life-size statues of Japanese astronauts and the Beatles.
(The statues looked a little weird, if you ask me!)
The fourth floor has a small arcade for kids, and tourists are allowed on FootTown's roof. Guess what's up there—an amusement park!
There's also a space that features street performers, just like the performers you might see on the streets below.
So there’s a lot for tourists to do here, and I haven’t even started telling you about the attractions within the tower itself yet!
Once you enter Tokyo Tower, you can either climb 590 stairs or take the elevator to the Main Observatory’s first floor.
At 150 meters, you are only about halfway up the tower, but Mr. Fay said it feels like you're already pretty high up.
As you walk around to check out the 360-degree view of Tokyo, your eyes will probably be drawn outward to the busy city.
But don’t forget to look down too! There's a window built into the floor that lets you see 150 meters below.
It’s pretty neat to look down at the sidewalk so far below, but I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone who is afraid of heights!
While you're in the Main Observatory, you might get to meet Tawabo, the tower's most unique employee.
Tawabo speaks four languages: Japanese, Korean, English, and Chinese.
Do you want to know why Tawabo is unique? He's a robot!
And get this—there’s also a music lounge on the first floor.
I guess it makes sense that the tower transmitting Tokyo’s television and radio stations would have some live performances of its own.
From the second floor of the Main Observatory, if it's a clear day, you might be able to see Mt. Fuji, Japan’s tallest and most sacred mountain.
And you’ll surely see the Sumida River running through the city, along with the Imperial Palace.
Tucked amid the concrete skyscrapers are the traditional clay-tile roofs of Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines.
But the highest Shinto shrine of all sits right there in Tokyo Tower.
With two claps and a bow, you can pray for love, safety, and even success on your exams at school!
Then—if you want to climb even higher—you can go up to the tower's Special Observatory.
The Special Observatory lets you view the city from 250 meters in the sky.
Mr. Fay said the night view from up there is pretty special.
All the angles and architecture of the city disappear into the dark, and the headlights from moving cars turn roads into rivers of light.
In 2012 a new broadcast tower—Tokyo Skytree—was completed.
The new tower is about twice as tall as Tokyo Tower, but Mr. Fay says he thinks the first tower will always have a special place in the hearts of Japanese people.
After taking the virtual tour, I agree with Mr. Fay. Tokyo Tower is a symbol of Japanese pride.
And there's so much cool stuff to do there, people will probably continue to visit it for many years to come.
Hey! I’m going to log back in to the tour and revisit the hologram museum.
Wait, did I forget to tell you about the tower's hologram museum? I guess you’ll have to check it out yourself. See you later!
Hello, everyone. It's Melissa. Today was Bring-Your-Child-to-Work day.

It was really fun but pretty tiring too!
My mom told me some cool things about Wall Street today, but I had already learned some facts from Mr. Fay's landmarks lesson.
Mr. Fay told us that the area called Wall Street is located at the southern end of Manhattan.
It's also one of the world's busiest financial centers. In fact, millions of dollars are traded there every single day!
Wall Street has been around for hundreds of years. In 1653 the lower end of Manhattan Island was a Dutch settlement called New Amsterdam.
But British colonists wanted the land too, so the Dutch built a wooden wall to protect themselves from possible attack.
Near the wall was a path, which eventually became known as "Wall Street."
We asked Mr. Fay how this narrow path grew into such a mighty symbol of financial power.
He said that in the late 1700s, New York City was a main center of trading and commerce.
Back then a small group of traders used to meet under a buttonwood tree at 68 Wall Street to trade stocks, or shares, of companies they owned.
In 1792, 24 of these traders signed the Buttonwood Agreement, promising to trade stocks only with each other.
They also set some basic rules for how trading should be done.
In 1817 this group officially became the New York Stock and Exchange Board.
Today it's known as the New York Stock Exchange.
After the establishment of the New York Stock Exchange, more banks and financial institutions moved to the area.
Eventually "Wall Street" came to mean not just the street but also the entire financial district in lower Manhattan.
If you've ever been to Wall Street and the rest of the financial district, you know it's a busy place, with businesspeople darting in and out of subway stations and tall, shiny office buildings.
As my mom and I walked around, she had to warn me several times to watch where I was going!
Wall Street has lots of tall modern buildings, but there are also some older historic ones.
First built in 1698, Trinity Church was one of the first church congregations established in America.
Back when Manhattan was the nation's first capital, a building called Federal Hall housed the government offices.
Federal Hall was where America's first president—George Washington—was sworn into office.
I bet you've seen photos of a popular tourist attraction on Wall Street—the famous charging bull.
Apparently an artist created this huge bronze statue in 1989 and installed it one winter night in front of the New York Stock Exchange.
There was an economic recession going on at the time, and the artist wanted to cheer up discouraged New Yorkers.
So he sculpted "Charging Bull" as a special holiday gift.
My mom took my picture in front of the bull, and I rubbed its nose for good luck because it's supposed to represent financial prosperity.
(Hey! Do you think my parents will finally raise my allowance now?)
Throughout its history, Wall Street has been associated with America's wealth and prosperity.
But Mr. Fay reminded us that Wall Street has also been associated with periods of economic decline.
When the American stock market crashed in 1929, it triggered the Great Depression.
Millions of people lost their jobs, and devastating poverty spread around the world.
Another U.S. stock market crash came in 2008.
A recession swept the globe, and many people blamed Wall Street for starting it by using risky lending practices to make lots of money.
By 2011 the "Occupy" movement had sprung up, with people around the world occupying city parks to protest greed in the financial industry.
As a symbol of wealth and prosperity, Wall Street has also been the target of violence.
In 1920 a bomb exploded on a street corner, killing 38 people.
In 1993 terrorists detonated a bomb in the World Trade Center's underground parking lot.
Then, on September 11, 2001, terrorists flew two planes into the twin towers of the World Trade Center.
The towers were destroyed, and thousands of people were murdered.
Today at the World Trade Center site, there's a memorial, a museum, and a new tower where the two once stood.
The new tower, known as One World Trade Center, is one of the tallest buildings in the world.
At the memorial Mom and I walked around two square pools, reading the names of the victims written in stone.
Today the New York Stock Exchange is one of the most famous places on Wall Street. In fact, it's the biggest stock exchange in the world.
My mom took me there, and the building's entrance is as grand as Mr. Fay said it was.
Six tall white columns support a giant marble sculpture over the doorway.
We took a tour of the building and looked down on the trading floor.
I've seen it before on TV, but it was pretty cool to see the real thing.
The floor was buzzing with activity as traders ran around, shouting and making deals.
I found out that each morning and afternoon, a bell is rung at the Stock Exchange to start and end the trading day.
Celebrities are often invited to ring the bell, so it's been clanged by astronauts, storm troopers from Star Wars, rock stars, even a duck from a TV commercial!
After our tour of the Stock Exchange, Mom and I left Wall Street and took the subway uptown.
We met my dad for dinner at a fancy restaurant. That was really fun too.

Hi, Little Fox readers! It's me, Jake, again.
I'm working on my Halloween costume; I'm going to dress up as a creepy grotesque this year.
Do you know what that is? I'd never heard of grotesques until this week's Landmarks lesson about Notre-Dame Cathedral.
Located in Paris, France, Notre-Dame is the most famous example of Gothic architecture from the Middle Ages.
I'll tell you about the grotesques at Notre-Dame in a few minutes. First I want to tell you about the cathedral itself!
Notre-Dame Cathedral was originally envisioned around 1160 by Maurice de Sully, the bishop of Paris.
By then the city of Paris had become the political and economic center of France.
De Sully decided to replace the ruins of two old churches with a huge cathedral dedicated to the Virgin Mary.
In fact, in French notre-dame means "our lady."
Construction of the cathedral began in 1163, and it was a massive undertaking.
A new road needed to be laid out to transport materials to the site, and houses were torn down to make room for the huge new building.
After more than 180 years, Notre-Dame was finally finished.
Gothic architecture is all about making people look up toward heaven, so a lot of Notre-Dame's elements seemed to reach toward the sky.
Rows of large columns and pointed arches allowed builders to make the ceilings really high.
And ribbed vaults were developed as a way to build a lightweight ceiling with heavy stone blocks.
That allowed walls to go much higher than those in earlier buildings.
Notre-Dame's high walls were filled with tall stained-glass windows that flooded the cathedral with beautiful, glowing light.
The windows told lots of different stories too.
You see, when Notre-Dame was being built, most people couldn't read.
So these windows showed scenes from the Old and New Testaments, allowing worshippers to "read" the stories through pictures instead of written words.
During construction, architects noticed that Notre-Dame's exterior walls were beginning to crack.
But they came up with a clever solution, something that was a new idea at the time: flying buttresses.
Those are supports, kind of like long arms, that extend out from the sides of the building and down to the ground.
Apparently the new flying buttresses weren't too popular at first; people thought they made the cathedral look ugly and unfinished.
But today flying buttresses are considered an important part of Gothic architecture.

Most people are familiar with Notre-Dame's west facade, which has three unique portals, or doorways, surrounded by intricate carvings that depict Mary's life, the Last Judgment, and the life of St. Anne.
Above these portals are statues of biblical kings.
Mr. Fay told us that the statues are actually replacements that were made in the 1800s because the originals were destroyed during the French Revolution.
The people attacking Notre-Dame thought the statues were French kings instead of biblical ones so they chopped the statues' heads off! The
most impressive part of the west facade is the pair of massive towers, which hold the cathedral's bells. Notre-Dame's
oldest bell, called Emmanuel, is in the South Tower. Emmanuel
weighs thirteen metric tons and is rung every hour and on special occasions. Okay,
now I can finally tell you about my favorite part of Notre-Dame—the grotesques! Some
of these awesome statues look down from the Grand Gallery, an outdoor balcony that connects the two towers. Grotesques
are strange figures—people or animals—with exaggerated or distorted features. Some
of Notre-Dame's grotesques look like scary demons, with sharp claws and fangs; others are chimeras, which are mythical creatures that have parts from two or more different animals. My
favorite statue at the cathedral is a winged monkey that looks like it's daydreaming as it looks out over the city. But
all of the statues are really cool; it's hard to imagine Notre-Dame without them! More
grotesques can be found in the form of gargoyles, or waterspouts. Mr.
Fay explained that rainwater can damage stone walls, so a network of gutters leads the water off the cathedral's roof and down to numerous gargoyles. Rainwater
rushes through the gutters and then spurts out of the grotesques' mouths, keeping the walls of Notre-Dame dry, and probably scaring lots of people too! It's
no wonder that Notre-Dame was the inspiration for Victor Hugo's famous novel The Hunchback of Notre-Dame .
The cathedral has played an important role in French history.
Crusaders prayed in it before going off to war and the famous emperor Napoleon had his coronation in it.
By 1768 Notre-Dame was such a well-known place, geographers decided to start using the cathedral to mark all distances in France!
As I mentioned before, the cathedral has also been attacked.
During the French Revolution, citizens ransacked it, stealing many of its treasures, and damaging parts of it.
Then in 1871, people who were angry with the French government attempted to burn down the cathedral.
Luckily, those people weren't successful, and Notre-Dame is still standing!
Mr. Fay told us that Notre-Dame continues to function as a cathedral and the center of Catholicism in France.
It can fit six thousand people and holds services every day, including a weekly televised service.
With about 13 million people visiting each year, Notre-Dame is the most popular tourist spot in France.
Visitors can light candles, pray to the Virgin Mary, check out the beautiful artwork, or listen to one of the cathedral's three pipe organs.
Visitors can even climb the 387 steps up to the Grand Gallery and get their picture taken next to a frightening grotesque.
Well, I should get back to work on my Halloween costume now. I have a lot to do if I want to look as cool as the grotesques at Notre-Dame!
